outcome_measurement_quality: high

effect_estimate: Of 56 water-management groups with complete data: 25 (44.6%) used proportional-equality payment (fee scaled to livestock owned), 7 (12.5%) an attenuated proportional form, and 24 (42.9%) numerical equality (flat fee per household regardless of usage). Active state/NGO involvement (regular visits, on-site presence) was significantly associated with communities adopting proportional equality (phi = -0.478, P = 0.000); without active state involvement, three intra-community dynamics (administration/counting costs, wealth/bargaining power of large herd-owners, and multiplex kinship-based sharing norms) pushed communities toward numerical equality instead. Proportional equality was significantly associated with higher satisfaction/success on every indicator measured: satisfaction with the institutional rules themselves (rank-biserial correlation rbc = 0.559, P = 0.000), with water point committee work (rbc = 0.427, P = 0.017), with community cooperation (rbc = 0.406, P = 0.006), and with general water-management satisfaction (rbc = 0.389, P = 0.003). No significant association was found between the payment rule and the technological infrastructure's susceptibility to failure (phi = -0.01, n.s.), suggesting the satisfaction effect is social/institutional rather than a proxy for better-performing boreholes. An agent-based simulation (calibrated on 80 households' actual livestock distribution; Gini = 0.49 for livestock ownership) projected that under numerical equality (flat fee, all pay the same regardless of usage), a rich household's share of total water usage rose from an already-disproportionate baseline to about 18 times a poor household's share after 100 months, while the livestock-ownership Gini coefficient rose further over the same period -- i.e., poor and moderately-well-off households' flat payments effectively subsidize both the current water consumption and the future wealth accumulation of richer households under the numerical-equality regime.

effect_estimate: Between 1997 and 2007 the Montes de Maria region recorded 56 massacres, ~220 civilian deaths (80% attributed to paramilitary violence), and more than 200,000 cases of forced displacement, producing the dispossession of over 80,000 hectares of land. The authors document that dispossession was sustained not only through violent coercion but through the combined, everyday use of coercive and legal/juridical strategies ('del rifle y el titulo' -- the rifle and the title): violently displaced land and water sources were subsequently legalized and formally titled, integrating them rapidly into land/water markets and large agribusiness development projects. effect_estimate: The 2014-2015 Sao Paulo drought exhausted the Cantareira System's useful reservoir volume by July 11, 2014, forcing sequential use of technical 'dead volume' reserves through February 2015. The PCJ river-basin committees, despite formal governance authority over basin planning, are described as failing to promote equitable water distribution among users during the crisis due to limited enforcement power. Government/utility communication about the crisis was also found to lack transparency (SABESP and state-government websites provided minimal or no public information on the Cantareira situation, per an Article 19 transparency assessment cited by the authors).

effect_estimate: The study traces Brazil's first sanitation and water-resource public policies from the Portuguese colonial period to the 1930s, showing that water regulation before the 19th century served primarily to facilitate economic extraction (sesmaria land/water grants for sugar-mill and mining operations) rather than public water-access provision. From the 18th-19th centuries, public fountains (chafarizes) -- financed through taxes on wine and cachaca plus judicial revenues, exemplified by Rio de Janeiro's Aqueduto da Carioca (completed 1750) -- provided nominally free and open community water access in colonial cities (Rio de Janeiro, Vila Rica, Salvador, Recife), but the actual transport of water from fountain to residence, and the collection/disposal of household excreta, was performed by enslaved people ('tigres'), meaning that practical, convenient in-home water access remained conditioned on the economic capacity to own or hire enslaved labor. The authors interpret this pattern, and Brazil's broader historical trajectory of centralized/fragmented, externally-dependent water-and-sanitation policy formation, through a dependency-theory lens emphasizing the country's structurally subordinate position in the international economic system as a persistent constraint shaping domestic sanitation institution-building.

subnational_unit: Hubli-Dharwad twin cities, Karnataka (8 pilot continuous-water-supply wards matched against 8 intermittent-supply control wards)
service_provider: Hubli-Dharwad Municipal Corporation, under the Karnataka Urban Water Supply and Sanitation Improvement Project (KUWASIP), World Bank-financed
regulatory_model: municipal water-tariff and service-level regulatory reform: a new increasing block volumetric tariff plus fixed flat rate and meter charge for the continuous-water-supply (CWS) pilot zone, replacing the intermittent-water-supply (IWS) flat-rate/free-standpipe tariff regime across the rest of the city
population: households in Hubli-Dharwad (~4,000-household panel surveyed over 4 rounds, 15 months)
income_group: all wealth quintiles (household socioeconomic score via principal component analysis of housing materials/assets, categorised into quintiles)

effect_estimate: Upgrading from intermittent (IWS) to continuous water supply (CWS) in a World Bank-financed pilot (KUWASIP) covering 10% of Hubli-Dharwad's wards nearly doubled average monthly household water-related monetary expenditure -- driven almost entirely by higher water bills under the new increasing-block CWS tariff structure -- but this was more than offset by reduced coping costs and amortised reductions in household water-storage-equipment investment, plus an average 22.5 hours/month per-household time saving from no longer needing to wait for water under a rationed delivery schedule; net average household savings were approximately Rs69/month, reported as robust and statistically significant across all wealth quintiles after econometric controls for socioeconomic confounders. However, the tariff burden was regressive: the two lowest wealth quintiles paid, on average, just over 3% of reported household income toward water under CWS -- much higher than the roughly 1% paid by the same quintiles under IWS -- while the highest wealth quintile's expenditure share as a proportion of income did not change significantly. At the utility/system level, the authors' NPV analysis found the pilot itself yielded positive net benefits, but that the further water-supply-augmentation investment required to scale continuous service city-wide would substantially reduce the project's net present value, leaving the financial feasibility of full city-wide scale-up unclear.

citation: Archibong B (2018). Historical origins of persistent inequality in Nigeria. Oxford Development Studies 46(3):325-347.
service_provider: federal and local government administrations (differential jurisdiction over infrastructure types)
regulatory_model: Federal vs. locally administered public-service jurisdiction: potable water and improved sanitation access administered locally, while electricity access is federally administered; historical precolonial ethnic centralization and federal-local political bargaining shape differential investment
population: Nigerian households, national DHS sample by ethnic/geopolitical zone
effect_measure: group-weighted Gini coefficient (GGini) and group-weighted coefficient of variation, by ethnic/geopolitical zone and survey year
effect_estimate: Ethnic inequality in access to locally-administered services (potable water, improved sanitation) declined markedly over time -- GGini for improved sanitation access fell from 0.3 (2003) to about 0.1 (2013); GGini for potable water access fell from 0.15 (2003) to 0.05 (2013) -- with the historically lagging Northwest and Northeast zones converging toward the national average. In contrast, ethnic inequality in the federally-administered electricity-access variable remained persistent (GGini rising from 0.1 to 0.2, 2008-2013), consistent with the paper's central finding that federal/local administrative jurisdiction, not just resource availability, predicts convergence versus persistence of access inequality. National mean potable-water access rose from 0.4 to 0.6 of households (2003-2013); mean improved-sanitation access rose from 0.2 to 0.5.
extraction_sample_size: Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) household data, 1990-2013 (5 survey rounds)
adjusted_or_unadjusted: both (descriptive Gini/CV trends plus regression tests of precolonial-centralization and local-government-quality mechanisms)
covariates: precolonial ethnic centralization (Murdock Ethnographic Atlas), local government quality, DHS survey year, ethnic/geopolitical zone
model_type: group-weighted inequality decomposition (Gini, coefficient of variation) plus regression analysis of historical-institutional mechanisms
study_design: quasi-experimental (repeated cross-sectional panel with historical-institutional identification strategy)
selection_bias: Low (DHS is a nationally representative repeated cross-sectional survey)
measurement_bias: Low (DHS binary water/sanitation access indicators are standardized and validated)
confounding: Moderate (precolonial centralization measure has known historical-dating debates, acknowledged by the author; local-government-quality mechanism partially observational)
attrition: Not applicable (repeated independent cross-sections, not a panel of the same households)
reporting_bias: Low (persistent electricity-access inequality reported alongside converging water/sanitation inequality, not selectively favorable)

citation: Marcatelli M (2015). Suspended redistribution: 'green economy' and water inequality in the Waterberg, South Africa. Third World Quarterly 36(12):2244-2258.
service_provider: private game farms and nature reserves (self-supplied); Vaalwater/Leseding municipal water service
regulatory_model: Private water use on game farms and nature reserves is conceived and managed as a private commodity deriving from land ownership, largely exempted from state water regulation, while the nearby town of Vaalwater and township of Leseding experience unmet minimum water-provision standards
population: black and poor residents of Leseding township, relocated from private farms and rural villages
tenure_status: displaced former farm workers/dwellers relocated to informal settlements or rural towns
effect_measure: qualitative ethnographic case-study findings

citation: Murebwayire M.L., Nilsson E., Nhapi I., Wali U.G. (2025). A Systematic Review of Households' Fecal Sludge Management Situation to Identify Gaps and Improve Services: A Case of Kigali City, Rwanda. Sustainability.
service_provider: private FSM operators, WASAC (utility), City of Kigali/district authorities
regulatory_model: PRISMA-2020 systematic review synthesizing 36 scientific studies and 32 government/policy documents (laws, national strategies, regulations, policies, standards and guidelines) on household-level fecal sludge management (FSM) in Kigali, organized around four themes: access to sanitation, FSM services, public health, and sanitation governance

tenure_status: renters and landlords in disputes over pit-latrine/on-site sanitation maintenance responsibility

effect_estimate: Reviewing 23 government publications (laws, national strategies, regulations, policies, standards and guidelines), the study finds Kigali's sanitation governance fragmented across overlapping institutional mandates (national ministries, WASAC, City of Kigali/district authorities, and private FSM operators), with unclear division of enforcement responsibility. Regulatory/building-law approval requirements for on-site sanitation facilities exist on paper but are documented as seldom implemented or enforced in practice. Authorities are found to prioritize sanctions (fines, condemnation notices) over supportive regulatory mechanisms when addressing non-compliant household sanitation facilities, leaving poorer households -- who cannot afford compliant upgrades -- exposed to punitive enforcement rather than accommodation. A secondary finding cited from the reviewed literature is that poorer and less-educated families are less likely to gain admittance to shared/public sanitation facilities. The WASH sector overall faces an estimated annual funding gap of USD 316 million, with only approximately 7% of the sector budget allocated to sanitation, constraining both infrastructure investment and regulatory enforcement capacity.

The Law on Drinking Water and Wastewater (N1633, 2019) mandates the government as guarantor of access, and Resolution #679 (2011) assigns SUE KMK implementation authority. citation: Millington N., Scheba S. (2020). Day Zero and The Infrastructures of Climate Change: Water Governance, Inequality, and Infrastructural Politics in Cape Town's Water Crisis. International Journal of Urban and Regional Research.
service_provider: City of Cape Town Water and Sanitation Department
regulatory_model: Qualitative political-ecology case study (semi-structured interviews with 4 mid/high-ranking City of Cape Town Water and Sanitation Department officials plus civil-society/academic respondents, participant observation of crisis-response meetings/forums, and discourse analysis of city documents/media) of Cape Town's 2015-2018 'Day Zero' water crisis, examining the withdrawal of universal Free Basic Water (FBW) provision, indigent-registration-conditioned FBW eligibility, mandatory Water Management Device (WMD/prepaid meter) installation that automatically restricts supply once the FBW allocation is exhausted, and revised stepped water tariff structures introduced in response to the drought's financial pressures
population: Cape Town residents, particularly indigent/low-income households subject to FBW registration and WMD installation
effect_measure: qualitative case study (interview analysis, participant observation, document/discourse analysis)
effect_estimate: Since South Africa's 2001 FBW policy, municipalities are constitutionally/statutorily required to provide a minimum 25 litres/person/day (6 kl/household/month) FBW, with the only legal requirement being the guarantee of FBW to REGISTERED indigent households -- a formal registration process the authors describe as 'arduous,' requiring residents to prove their status (e.g. presenting an ID book), which effectively excludes many poor and vulnerable people, especially those in the informal economy for whom the documentation cost is 'almost impossible.' In July 2017 the city made FBW entirely dependent on indigent registration (previously universal for the first 6 kl), and expanded WMD installation from roughly 250,000 installed by 2018 (largely in homes deemed indigent) at a rate increased to 2,000 devices/week during the crisis. WMDs automatically restrict/cut off water supply once the allocated quantity (350 litres/household/day under WMD, later 10.5 kl/7.35 kl for registered indigent households) is exhausted; the devices were declared legal following the Constitutional Court's Mazibuko ruling. A 2012 Environmental Monitoring Group study found a 'high incidence of technical failures leading to cut-offs, recurrent leaks leading to the allocated litres running out quickly, a poor consultation process, and slow response times.' A representative of the Western Cape Water Caucus stated indigent registration 'will inevitably exclude poor households who could benefit' and described it as requiring 'an SA ID [book], you have to jump through all of hoops.' New tariff structures (July 2018) introduced a fixed service charge plus restriction-linked block tariffs; comparing Level 3 restrictions in December 2016 to December 2018, the cost per kilolitre for the first 6 kl increased from R0 to R15.73, and from R16.54 to R22.38 for the 6-10.5 kl block.

subnational_unit: 31 Texas counties along the Texas-Mexico border
service_provider: local water/wastewater utilities and special districts, with funding from TWDB, USDA, Texas Department of Agriculture (TDA), and North American Development Bank (NADB)
regulatory_model: Mixed-methods retrospective program evaluation (geographically weighted regression on $626 million in wastewater infrastructure funding across 31 counties plus over 100 interviews with utilities and program managers) of first-time wastewater service extension to Texas colonias (informal border settlements historically lacking water/sewer infrastructure) from 1995-2017, examining the historical absence of county land-use enforcement that enabled colonia formation, subsequent Model Subdivision Rules (MSR) requiring counties to adopt land-use regulation to prevent further unserviced-lot proliferation, permit/inspection requirements for onsite septic systems, and household-connection-cost subsidy design within infrastructure grants

effect_estimate: Before 1989, Texas counties lacked authority to require subdivision rules preventing developers from subdividing and selling lots without water/wastewater infrastructure; the absence of city/county enforcement of land-use planning or building codes in colonias located in extraterritorial jurisdictions or unincorporated county areas 'further exacerbated non-compliant growth,' compounded by insufficient political clout from geographic remoteness and lower socioeconomic status. From 1987 to 2005 the Texas legislature passed laws requiring counties to adopt Model Subdivision Rules (MSRs) requiring water/wastewater/paved-road/drainage infrastructure before land could be subdivided or sold, aimed at preventing further colonia proliferation. Wastewater coverage of the colonia population increased from under 20% in 1995 to 77% by 2018, with $626 million invested in 119 wastewater projects across 27 counties funded primarily by TWDB (80%, $480 million), USDA, and TDA. GWR analysis found funding was generally distributed equitably relative to 1995 need (21 of 31 counties received the predicted funding amount); by 2018, 22 of 31 counties achieved the expected reduction in unserved population. Grant programs were redesigned to include household connection costs within the grant itself after early projects found many families could not afford thousands of dollars to connect their homes to the new system -- interviewed utilities confirmed this was 'very helpful' to project success, and residents were more likely to connect when the hookup subsidy was included. As an alternative to centralized connection for the most isolated remaining colonias (costly to reach, given distance/lack of institutional capacity), onsite systems require a permit application process (required in Texas) with inspections every two years where residents must provide proof of maintenance. Requirements to be completed before grant application could exceed eight years, and funding depends entirely on utilities/project sponsors having sufficient institutional capacity to apply -- rural systems were reported to be smaller and have more difficulty with the funding process.

In the Babati/eWater case, CBWSOs are responsible for determining the number and names of vulnerable households eligible for a monthly USD0.22-per-person free water credit allocation; over 91% (446/490) of surveyed households in Endanachan village used water for free (not registered as paying), while only 7% (36/490) paid cash per collection, and less than 50% of households were satisfied with the prepaid system. In Karatu, 71% (326/457) of households believed everyone can afford the water price, but 18% (131/457) stated the poorest household could not afford it, and there is no formal lifeline provision -- it is merely assumed vendors can provide access to vulnerable groups informally. Across all three cases, satisfaction with the prepaid systems was generally high (88% satisfied/very satisfied in Kishapu, 83% in Karatu) but tariff-setting involved political struggle between local leaders and NGO/donor proposals over acceptable price levels, and revenue accountability remained difficult to verify -- e.g. a mismatch was found between the Kishapu utility's online revenue database (~USD42,000 for 2018) and its official financial record (~USD24,000).

citation: Shah R., Badiger S. (2020). Conundrum or paradox: deconstructing the spurious case of water scarcity in the Himalayan Region through an institutional economics narrative. Water Policy.
service_provider: Darjeeling Municipality (DM) Water Works Department; Public Health and Engineering Department (PHED), Government of West Bengal; informal samaj self-help groups; private water suppliers
regulatory_model: Qualitative institutional-economics case study (topic-guided key-informant interviews with DM/PHED officials, focus group discussions, semi-structured household interviews, snowball/purposive sampling, and secondary municipal records/archives) of formal and informal water institutions in Darjeeling, India, examining the DM's formal household water-connection process (requiring a Khatian land-rights record, a land registration document, and a municipal mutation document as proof of residency, plus an application fee and a tiered connection charge), DM discretion over approving informal samaj requests for public standpipe installation, and political/institutional fragmentation of water governance across the DM, PHED, Gorkha Territorial Administration, Forest Department, and Indian Army
population: residents of Darjeeling Municipal Town, West Bengal, India (~132,000 population)
effect_measure: qualitative institutional case-study analysis (key-informant interviews, focus groups, and secondary municipal/administrative records)
effect_estimate: A formal household water connection in Darjeeling requires an application form (INR 100, USD1.50) accompanied by three supporting documents: a Khatian (record of rights for the land from the Land Reforms Department), a land registration document from the court, and a mutation document from the municipality as proof of residency. The connection charge is INR 17,000 (USD250), rising to INR 35,000 (USD520) for an immediate connection with additional labour/piping, plus an annual water fee of about INR 500 (USD7.50). Public standpipes, which have an increasing number of dependents who are mostly migrants without the ability to procure the required documentation, are less convenient and reliable than private connections. Only 10-15% of the population is covered by the formal municipal supply (Water Supply Coverage indicator = 15%, weekly water availability = 1 hour, revenue collection efficiency = 75%, 0% of connections metered); the remaining 85% depend on informal springs (managed by community samaj self-help groups) and private water suppliers (porters, hand-carts, tankers, and households selling surplus private-spring water). When a samaj requests a new public standpipe, the DM carries out feasibility checks and grants or denies permission for construction; installation cost is borne by either the DM or the samaj depending on negotiation and the samaj's political reach, and the DM apparently takes time to approve connection requests and is said to be facing a financial crunch that has shifted cost-bearing onto the samaj. Governance is fragmented across the DM (elected body), PHED (appointed engineers, State-run), the Gorkha Territorial Administration (autonomous hill council), the Forest Department, the Tea Board, and the Indian Army, each controlling land or infrastructure the water system depends on, producing 'political fragmentation' and 'issue-based fragmentation' that repeatedly stalled multiple augmentation-scheme proposals (Rambi Jhora, Khong Khola, Balasun River Scheme) over decades.

citation: Shrestha A., Joshi D., Roth D. (2020). The hydro-social dynamics of exclusion and water insecurity of Dalits in peri-urban Kathmandu Valley, Nepal: fluid yet unchanging. Contemporary South Asia.
service_provider: community-registered Drinking Water Supply and Sanitation User Committees (e.g. RDWSSC), Community Forest User Groups (CFUGs)
regulatory_model: Qualitative actor-oriented case study (74 key-informant interviews -- 44 men including 9 Dalits, 30 women including 14 Dalits -- with 41 conversational and 24 semi-structured interviews, snowball sampling, multiple interview rounds) of caste-based (Dalit) exclusion from water access in a peri-urban Kathmandu Valley village, examining prior-use water rights recognized informally and by law, formal registration of a Drinking Water Supply and Sanitation User Committee (RDWSSC) that controls access to a spring source, an annual water fee and additional membership fee charged to new in-migrants, Community Forest User Group (CFUG) membership (tied to land ownership) required to access water originating in community forest, and Nepal's official policy of mandatory proportionate representation of Dalits/marginalized groups on user-committee boards that resulted only in symbolic inclusion without real decision-making power
population: residents of Lamatar VDC (Tehrabise, Dandathok, Sisneri villages/hamlets), Kathmandu Valley, Nepal -- Dalit and higher-caste households
effect_measure: qualitative case-study analysis (interviews, direct quotations, and an actor-oriented analytical framework)
effect_estimate: Dalit (Sarki) households in Tehrabise hamlet historically held prior-use rights to the Raksidol spring, but when neighbouring Dandathok villagers formally registered a Raksidol Drinking Water Supply and Sanitation User Committee (RDWSSC) with NGO support in the mid-1990s, they excluded the closer Dalit-majority Tehrabise households from committee membership, instead including higher-caste households from a more distant village -- 'the decision of Dandathok residents to include higher-caste households from a rather distant village, instead of including the Dalit households in Tehrabise... suggests a conscious political strategy to avoid any possible prior-use right claims.' In 2008, RDWSSC began charging an annual water fee (USD4.84) plus an additional membership fee for new in-migrants (USD48.6). When Tehrabise later requested access as new formal members, they were told they would need to 'pay the same rate as new migrants to get water,' despite having used the source since generations; RDWSSC has instead 'closely monitored any damage to input pipelines by Tehrabise villagers' and denies access, saying 'those Sarki people do not ask permission to take water. When water is not sufficient for us, we simply dismantle their pipes.' Separately, access to a Kalidevi spring on the Patle Community Forest required Community Forest User Group (CFUG) membership, itself tied to land ownership within the forest boundary; official Nepali policy mandates the Patle CFUG committee include 50% female representatives and proportionate representation of poorer/lower-caste groups, and the committee does include two Dalit Tehrabise representatives, but 'it is evident... that these Tehrabise Dalit representatives were not involved in decision-making about this very institution' -- in 2016 a wealthy higher-caste in-migrant who bought land and paid a CFUG membership fee had a spring source reallocated to benefit his private household connection, with Tehrabise villagers left without meaningful input despite the water nominally being routed to benefit them.

Uganda's Public Health Act (1964, amended 2000) states that 'any dwelling without proper sanitation facilities [shall] be closed down and or its owner prosecuted,' with Part IV Articles 7(a) and 14(a) of the Local Governments Act (1997) providing for enforcement of building/maintenance standards for latrines; however, 'enforcement is limited due to weak public sector capacity and the absence of regulatory units in rural areas.' citation: Chidambaram S. (2020). How do institutions and infrastructure affect mobilization around public toilets vs. piped water? Examining intra-slum patterns of collective action in Delhi, India. World Development.
subnational_unit: four Jhuggi Jhopri Clusters (informal settlements), Delhi
service_provider: Delhi Jal Board (DJB); Delhi Urban Shelter Improvement Board (DUSIB); municipal corporations; Department of Railways (for one settlement on railway land)
regulatory_model: Qualitative ethnographic case study (repeated fieldwork visits January-April 2015, interviews with residents, NGO staff, DUSIB/DJB bureaucrats, slum leaders, and local politicians) of intra-slum variation in collective action around water versus toilets in four Delhi Jhuggi Jhopri Clusters (JJCs), examining India's official notified/non-notified legal classification of slums -- only notified slums are officially entitled to individual household water connections, while non-notified 'illegal' slums (constituting nearly 59% of all slums in Delhi) instead officially receive subsidized water only through community standposts -- informal 'quasi-legal' negotiated pipe-laying arrangements with DJB bureaucrats and elected MLAs, the risk of bureaucratic destruction of unauthorized private toilet-sewerage connections as 'illegal construction,' and jurisdictional fragmentation over toilet construction approval across DUSIB, DJB, the land-owning agency (which varies by settlement -- Delhi Development Authority, central government departments, or the Department of Railways), and municipal corporations
population: residents of four Jhuggi Jhopri Cluster informal settlements (700-1,000 households each) in Delhi, India
effect_measure: qualitative ethnographic case-study analysis (participant observation, semi-structured interviews, and direct quotations across four communities)
effect_estimate: Officially, non-notified slums (Jhuggi Jhopri Clusters) are not entitled to individual legal access to household piped water connections and instead officially receive subsidized water only through community standposts installed by DUSIB; unreliable supply and poor infrastructure in these communities is well documented in the literature. Despite this, residents across all four communities negotiated informal but bureaucratically 'authorized' (though not strictly legal) small-group ('gully') pipe connections to the DJB main line, requiring community members to pool INR 1,000-2,000 per household for pipes/taps, with the arrangement requiring implicit approval from DJB engineers and, where needed, lobbying of the locally elected MLA (since DJB falls under state-legislature purview). By contrast, private household toilets connected via pipes to open drains -- while common as a way to avoid poorly-functioning shared public toilet complexes -- run 'a significant risk of being discovered and destroyed by the bureaucratic agencies as "illegal construction"' since DUSIB (the parastatal responsible for toilet complexes) can only build once the appropriate land-owning agency has cleared land, creating a 'labyrinthine' multi-agency structure (DUSIB, DJB, land-owning agency, municipal corporation) with an 'extremely unclear' chain of command; in one settlement (SD2, on Railway Department land), the Railway Department itself threatened the entire settlement with eviction over a new toilet complex construction, and the complex was never made functional. The study finds that water access, unlike toilet access, was successfully converted from a public good into a smaller-group 'club good,' making negotiated informal DJB pipe connections more tractable and politically viable (easier bureaucratic/jurisdictional simplicity, since DJB is the sole agency with authority) than toilet infrastructure, which requires costly, multi-agency, harder-to-informally-authorize approvals.

citation: Fischer A., Hope R., Manandhar A., Hoque S., Foster T., Hakim A., Islam M.S., Bradley D. (2020). Risky responsibilities for rural drinking water institutions: The case of unregulated self-supply in Bangladesh. Global Environmental Change.
service_provider: Department of Public Health and Engineering (DPHE); Union Parishads (local government); private drillers/mistri (informal self-supply market)
regulatory_model: Mixed-methods infrastructure-audit study (water-point-level blanket inventories across ten Matlab villages and five Khulna/Polder-29 unions, combined with secondary DPHE project cost archives and Bayesian machine-learning growth modeling) of the shift in Bangladesh's rural drinking-water sector from a regulated collective public-provision model to an unregulated private self-supply market, examining the historical DPHE requirement that publicly funded tubewells be allocated only to collectives of ten or more individuals who formally applied as a group (with independent water-quality testing for each new public installation), decentralization of tubewell-siting decisions from central agencies to sub-district (upazila) and Union Parishad local government, and the complete absence of drilling permits, registration, licensing, or water-quality regulation for the now-dominant private self-supply market
population: rural households in Matlab (Chandpur District) and Polder 29 (Khulna Division), Bangladesh
effect_measure: Bayesian Gaussian-process growth modeling of tubewell infrastructure counts, mean-crowding density metrics, and secondary DPHE cost-archive time-series analysis
effect_estimate: Between 2012 and 2017, an estimated forty-five unregulated private tubewells were installed for every one publicly funded tubewell installed by government. The household-to-tubewell ratio in Matlab declined from 57.5 in 1982 to 1.6 by 2017, approaching market saturation; nationally, in 2018 households were estimated to have invested up to USD253 million in tubewells, representing nearly 65% of total national water-and-sanitation-sector household-level finance (per GLAAS data). Historically, publicly funded tubewells required a formal group application (ten or more individuals who agreed the water point would be available to the whole group) processed through a defined tender procedure, with independent water-quality testing required for each new public installation since 2012 -- providing one, albeit unmonitored-after-installation, form of regulation. As government relinquished control over supply chains, informal private local well-drillers (mistri) who install shallow tubewells (under thirty metres deep) are not regulated or licensed. Real (inflation-adjusted) prices for both publicly and privately installed shallow tubewells fell substantially between 1982 and 2017 (roughly 70% decrease for private, 43% for public), with private household investment growing as a share of total national WASH-sector finance and remaining almost entirely outside any formal regulatory, monitoring, or safety-testing framework -- unlike public water points, there are no drilling permits, no registration requirements, and no compliance testing for the private self-supply market that now provides the overwhelming majority of rural water infrastructure.
extraction_sample_size: water-infrastructure audits across 10 Matlab villages (3,830 water points, 3,734 domestic) and 5 Khulna/Polder-29 unions (2,805 tubewells, 19 pond sand filters); secondary DPHE project cost archive (150 unique budget items, 67 projects, 1980-2016)
adjusted_or_unadjusted: not applicable (Bayesian growth-trend modeling and descriptive infrastructure-audit/cost-archive analysis, not a covariate-adjusted regression)
model_type: Bayesian Gaussian-process growth modeling combined with mean-crowding density metrics and secondary cost-archive trend analysis
study_design: mixed-methods infrastructure-audit study (quantitative blanket water-point inventories, Bayesian growth modeling, and secondary document/cost-archive analysis)
selection_bias: Low-moderate (blanket enumeration of all water points in purposively selected villages/unions, not a nationally representative sample; ten Matlab villages selected on flood-embankment location and infrastructure heterogeneity criteria)
measurement_bias: Low (direct field-based water-point audits with trained enumerators, cross-validated against longitudinal icddr,b household survey data spanning multiple decades)
confounding: Not applicable (descriptive growth-trend and cost-archive analysis, not seeking to isolate causal effects)
reporting_bias: Low (paper explicitly frames the unregulated growth as a policy risk/gap rather than a success story, discussing both the private-market benefits for coverage and the regulatory/safety risks)
legal_measurement_quality: high (documents specific DPHE group-application/tender requirements, national policy documents -- 1998 National Policy for Safe Water Supply and Sanitation, 2004/2011 Sector Development Plans -- and the explicit absence of drilling permit/registration/licensing regulation for private self-supply)
outcome_measurement_quality: high (blanket water-point infrastructure audits across two independently studied regions, cross-validated against decades of longitudinal household survey and DPHE administrative cost data)

citation: Enqvist J.P., Ziervogel G. (2019). Water governance and justice in Cape Town: An overview. WIREs Water.
service_provider: City of Cape Town Water and Sanitation Department; national Department of Water and Sanitation (DWS)
regulatory_model: Combined 'overview' and 'state-of-the-art' literature review (published academic articles plus City of Cape Town/government reports and informally-shared research community documents) of Cape Town's water governance and justice arrangements across the 2015-2018 drought, examining South Africa's 1997 Water Services Act, the 2001/2007/2014 Free Basic Water indigent-registration policy (25 litres/person/day or 6-10.5 kilolitres/household/month for registered indigent households), Water Management Devices (WMDs) installed from 2007 onward that cap usage and cut supply on excess use, regressive block tariffs, the 2018 near-crisis 'Day Zero' disaster response plan and its three phases, and historical disconnection practices dating to the apartheid-era nonpayment protests
population: Cape Town residents, particularly low-income, colored, and Black township/informal-settlement households
effect_measure: narrative literature review/overview synthesis (published academic articles plus government/NGO reports and documents)
effect_estimate: South Africa's 2001 Free Basic Water (FBW) policy mandates a daily 25 litres/person or monthly 6 kilolitres/household (for a household of eight) at no cost, accessible no more than 200m from homes; 2007/2014 policy revisions acknowledged municipalities' limited implementation capacity and restricted the policy to registered indigent households, who receive a bumped-up allocation of 10.5 kilolitres/month if they agree to install a Water Management Device (WMD) -- though households may fail to register as indigent due to lack of awareness, inconvenience, socioeconomic restrictions, fear, or political motivations for remaining off-list. Regressive block tariffs charge higher per-litre rates for high-volume households, but this policy disproportionately punishes large low-income households (extended family/backyard shacks housing 15-30 people) that exceed the four-person-per-household assumption underlying the tariff structure; tariffs were changed in July 2017 to charge everyone but indigent households for even the most basic water needs. During apartheid, authorities cut off supply to indebted consumers, leaving some areas (usually Black African) without running water in 90% of households. WMDs, introduced from 2007, are described by the City as helping low-income households 'detect leaks and limit their use to what they could afford,' but have been criticized for being installed without free, prior, and informed consent from residents, with reports of residents being manipulated into signing forms accepting the WMD; those who later hire an independent plumber to bypass the device risk 'breaking a legal agreement.' The City's Critical Water Shortages Disaster Plan (October 2017) outlined 3 phases -- Preservation Restrictions, Disaster Restrictions ('Day Zero,' triggering strict rationing and forced turn-off of most private taps), and Disaster Implementation -- with WMD installations ramped up throughout targeting wealthier high-volume households over 10.5 kilolitres/month as the crisis progressed. Level 6B restrictions (February 2018) limited the daily allowance to 50 litres/person before Day Zero was pushed back following winter rains.
extraction_sample_size: literature review/overview synthesis (published academic articles plus government/NGO reports and grey literature)
model_type: narrative literature review and policy-document synthesis
study_design: narrative overview/state-of-the-art review (not a systematic review with documented search methodology)
selection_bias: Not applicable in the conventional empirical sense (a narrative overview synthesizing published academic literature plus government/NGO documents and grey literature, explicitly not a systematic/replicable review)
measurement_bias: Low (triangulates published peer-reviewed academic literature with primary City of Cape Town policy/disaster-plan documents and secondary media reporting)
confounding: Not applicable (narrative synthesis, not an empirical causal design)
reporting_bias: Low (paper explicitly foregrounds water justice/inequality as a central critical lens, reporting both the City's stated intentions and documented failures such as WMD consent issues and tariff regressivity)
legal_measurement_quality: high (directly analyzes South Africa's 1997 Water Services Act, the 1998 Water Act's community-participation requirements, the 2001/2007/2014 FBW indigent policy revisions, and City disaster-plan/by-law documents)
outcome_measurement_quality: high (synthesizes multiple independent empirical sources -- household surveys, smart-meter data studies, City administrative reports -- cited throughout, rather than presenting new primary data of its own)

citation: Adank M., Godfrey S., Butterworth J., Defere E. (2019). Small town water services sustainability checks: development and application in Ethiopia. Water Policy.
subnational_unit: Adishihu (Tigray), Sheno (Oromia), Maksegnit (Amhara), Abomsa (Oromia), Welenchiti (Oromia), Kebridehar (Somali), Wukro (Tigray)
service_provider: Town Water Utilities (TWUs), overseen by Water Boards, Town Administrations, and Regional Water Bureaux
regulatory_model: Mixed-methods diagnostic sustainability-check framework (household survey of 100 households per town, water point survey, key-informant interviews with Regional Water Bureau/Town Water Utility staff) applied to 7 small towns' piped water schemes, examining Ethiopia's Town Water Board governance structure established via regional proclamations with limited formal accountability to town administrations, absence of a national/regional urban water regulatory agency, tariff-approval authority resting with town administrations, and the near-total absence (except Wukro) of shared yard-connection provisions allowing low-income households in compound housing to jointly apply for and pay for a water connection
population: residents of 7 small Ethiopian towns (populations 10,771-49,925)
effect_measure: standardized diagnostic sustainability-check scoring (0-100 ordinal indicator scores across institutional, technical, financial, environmental, and social sustainability domains) combined with household/water-point survey data
effect_estimate: All 7 Town Water Utilities scored 25/100 (below the 50-point benchmark) on the 'urban poor get affordable water' social-sustainability indicator (SP-S-1), the lowest average score of any indicator assessed (average 25, 0% of towns meeting the benchmark). All towns except Wukro provided services to the poor exclusively through public taps/standpipes, with none of the other 6 utilities making provision for shared yard connections that would allow the urban poor living in compound housing to jointly apply and pay for an individual connection; even in Wukro, shared connections were allowed but the number of public taps remained very limited. On the national enabling-environment indicator N-I-3 (urban regulatory agency), Ethiopia scored 0/100 -- 'no regulatory agency' exists for urban water services. Town Water Boards (established under regional proclamations for towns with populations below 100,000) are officially accountable to town administrations, but in reality 'there are no performance agreements between a Water Board and a town administration and therefore limited formal accountability between the two'; the town administration's main role is approving tariffs and providing match-funding for scheme expansion. Piped-scheme coverage ranged from 27% (Kebridehar, where 66% of residents instead depend on tanker-truck-filled household storage) to 99% (Welenchiti, Wukro). None of the 7 towns met the GTP-2 norm of 16 hours/day of uninterrupted water supply (reliability score = 0 in all towns).

citation: Hoque S.F., Hope R., Arif S.T., Akhter T., Naz M., Salehin M. (2019). A social-ecological analysis of drinking water risks in coastal Bangladesh. Science of the Total Environment.
subnational_unit: Polder 29 (Duramia and Batiaghata upazilas, Khulna District)
service_provider: Union Parishads; local government-led/NGO-supported piped systems; private tubewell owners/vendors; Department of Public Health Engineering (DPHE)
regulatory_model: Mixed-methods social-ecological systems study (2,103 household surveys, water infrastructure audit of 2,805 tubewells and 19 pond sand filters, 6 focus group discussions, 13 key-informant interviews) of governance and institutional risks to drinking water security in a coastal Bangladeshi polder, examining Union Parishad institutional capacity limits for managing complex piped schemes, a failed formal water-vending tariff system that could not recover costs, elite-influenced/nepotistic allocation of public deep tubewells across unions, absence of formal regulation or oversight of the rapidly growing private self-supply tubewell market, and cross-upazila jurisdictional boundary issues that left one union unable to benefit from formal government water arrangements available elsewhere in the polder
population: households in Polder 29, coastal Khulna District, Bangladesh (58,000 population, 17,000 households)
effect_measure: descriptive household-survey/infrastructure-audit statistics (2,103 households, 2,805-tubewell census) combined with qualitative FGD/KII analysis and principal component analysis for wealth classification
effect_estimate: The number of privately-funded tubewells increased four-fold in the past decade, comprising 78% of all tubewells in the polder by 2018 (versus a ~4% population growth over the same period); despite self-supply's dominance, it is 'not recognised nor regulated as a formal service delivery model,' with no water-quality testing, drilling permits, or monitoring after installation. Disproportionate allocation of government-funded tubewells was observed across unions -- Union-4 had a notably higher number of public tubewells per person than Union-5, attributed in part to nepotism/elite capture in siting decisions (citing van Geen et al. 2016) alongside genuine aquifer-availability differences. A formal electricity-powered piped-vending system in Union-4 (established 2015 via the Upazila Governance and Development Project fund) suffered institutional failures across three years: tariffs were set too low to recover operational costs (salaries, fuel, maintenance); the system supplied free water to the entire southern region for three months during a mid-2015 flood regardless of subscription status; a newly-elected union chairman promised 'free water for all' resulting in villagers refusing to pay tariffs, with the management committee only receiving a nominal collected amount via a third person; and the truck-based delivery system eventually suffered irreparable damage in an accident, ceasing operation due to lack of repair funds. By contrast, a community-managed electric piped system in Union-3 (NGO-supported, with a volunteer tariff-collecting committee with high ownership/engagement) operated more effectively but faced continuous political pressure from the union chairman to expand free coverage to unserved communities in a way that would jeopardise system sustainability. Since Union-5 fell under the jurisdiction of a different upazila than the rest of the polder, the area struggled to benefit from water-source arrangements available through formal government channels elsewhere in the polder. Significant wealth-based and gendered disparities in water access were also documented: 60% of rich households versus 15% of extreme-poor households used vended water as their main source in high-salinity sites, with poorer households instead relying on pond sand filters or walking 1-3 km to fetch water from distant tubewells.
extraction_sample_size: 2,103 households (978 phase 1, 1,125 phase 2 across 16 mouzas); water infrastructure audit of 2,805 tubewells and 19 pond sand filters; 6 focus group discussions; 13 key-informant interviews
adjusted_or_unadjusted: not applicable (descriptive survey/audit statistics and qualitative analysis, principal component analysis used only for wealth classification)
model_type: descriptive social-ecological systems analysis (household survey, infrastructure audit, PCA-based wealth classification, and qualitative FGD/KII analysis)
study_design: mixed-methods case study (descriptive quantitative household/infrastructure survey plus qualitative focus groups and key-informant interviews)
selection_bias: Low-moderate (stratified random household sampling across 16 mouzas via random route/walk method with 15 trained enumerators; complete water infrastructure audit rather than a sample)
measurement_bias: Low (in-situ salinity testing of all functional tubewells/pond sand filters, ONA electronic household survey, hydrogeological borelog mapping using DPHE data at 31 locations)
confounding: Not applicable (descriptive social-ecological systems analysis, not a causal regression design)
reporting_bias: Low (paper explicitly documents institutional failures -- the failed vending system, elite-capture allocation concerns, political pressure undermining sustainability -- alongside successes)
legal_measurement_quality: high (documents Union Parishad institutional mandate/capacity limits, DPHE's regulatory role, absence of formal regulation for private self-supply, and cross-jurisdictional boundary effects on service access)
outcome_measurement_quality: high (2,103-household survey combined with a complete water-point infrastructure census of 2,805 tubewells and detailed hydrogeological mapping)

citation: Appiah-Effah E., Duku G.A., Azangbego N.Y., Aduafo Aggrey R.K., Gyapong-Korsah B., Nyarko K.B. (2019). Ghana's post-MDGs sanitation situation: an overview. Journal of Water, Sanitation and Hygiene for Development.
service_provider: Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies (MMDAs); Ministry of Sanitation and Water Resources (MSWR); Environmental Health and Sanitation Directorate (EHSD)
regulatory_model: Policy review (eight-step policy analysis framework applied to national policy/strategy documents, JMP/GSS coverage data, and published literature) of Ghana's post-MDGs sanitation situation, examining the Local Government Act (Act 462) assigning MMDAs statutory responsibility for sanitation services, the National Environmental Sanitation Policy's designation of sanitation as households' own financial responsibility, a novel 10% sanitation surcharge on property tax piloted in Ga West Municipal Assembly, absence of a national urban sanitation regulatory strategy, and planned creation of a National Sanitation Authority with regulatory/standard-setting powers
population: Ghanaian households, national sanitation sector
effect_measure: narrative policy-document synthesis combined with secondary national coverage statistics (JMP, GSS)
effect_estimate: Ghana's basic sanitation coverage increased only 4 percentage points during the MDG era (11% in 2000 to 15% in 2015), against a 54% MDG target, and stood at 21% by 2018 (17% rural, 25% urban); over 13 million Ghanaians (45%) rely on shared sanitation facilities, and 22% still practise open defecation. The National Environmental Sanitation Policy makes households responsible for financing their own household sanitation facilities, but improved household toilets meeting WHO/JMP standards cost up to US$1,000 to install -- representing between 29% and 66% of the average annual household income for the three lowest income quintiles -- a cost the authors identify as 'prohibitive for low-income households.' Government WASH-sector budget allocation fell from 0.66% of GDP (2012) to 0.15% of GDP (2017), and donor WASH funding inflows declined by two-thirds between 2008 and 2011. In response, the Ga West Municipal Assembly (GWMA), a district of Greater Accra, approved a novel 10% surcharge on property rate in October 2016 (effective January 2017), 'ring-fenced for sanitation services within the Municipality,' generating GHS 30,365 in revenue by end of 2018, though 'there was no record to show whether this has significantly contributed to increasing access to sanitation services.' The Local Government Act (Act 462) is the main legal act assigning MMDAs responsibility for sanitation services, and the Local Government Service Act provides technical assistance to MMDAs, but governance is fragmented across the Ministry of Sanitation and Water Resources (policy), the Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development/Environmental Health and Sanitation Directorate (implementation support), and 110+ MMDAs (local implementation), with plans -- not yet realized -- to create a National Sanitation Authority with a formal regulatory function and management of a National Sanitation Fund.

citation: Domínguez Serrano J., Castillo Pérez E. (2018). Las organizaciones comunitarias del agua en el estado de Veracruz. Análisis a la luz de la experiencia latinoamericana [Community water organizations in the state of Veracruz. Analysis in light of the Latin American experience]. Estudios Demográficos y Urbanos.
subnational_unit: Veracruz (Xalapa metropolitan zone, Emiliano Zapata, Tlalnehuayocan, Coatepec municipalities)
service_provider: Comisión Estatal de Agua del Estado de Veracruz (CAEV); OCSAS/patronatos de agua (community water organizations); municipal governments
regulatory_model: Qualitative case study (semi-structured interviews and focus groups with rural water committee members, 2012 fieldwork; review of Conagua's rural-committee database 2009-2013; review of Veracruz's water regulatory framework -- Ley Número 21 de Aguas del Estado de Veracruz-Llave and Ley 72 de Agua y Saneamiento) of community water organizations (organizaciones comunitarias de servicios de agua y saneamiento, OCSAS, locally called patronatos) in Veracruz, Mexico, examining the absence of formal legal recognition for community water organizations in Mexico -- unlike Chile, Ecuador, and several Central American countries where OCSAS have statutory recognition -- the 'municipal exclusivity' legal argument used by authorities to deny community organizations formal recognition, annual/short-term renewal requirements for rural water committees creating institutional instability, and CAEV's direct administration of rural systems in areas where municipal institutional capacity is absent
population: rural and peri-urban households served by community water organizations (patronatos/OCSAS) in Veracruz, Mexico
effect_measure: qualitative case-study analysis (semi-structured interviews, focus groups) combined with descriptive secondary administrative data (Conagua rural-committee database, CAEV inventory)
effect_estimate: Of Veracruz's 20,828 localities, 20,513 (98.5%) are rural (fewer than 2,500 inhabitants); CAEV estimates approximately 2,000 OCSAS exist statewide, of which 1,425 operate autonomously (autogestivas) and only 646 are formally administered by CAEV (2016 inventory). No Mexican federal or Veracruz state policy formally recognizes or grants legal status to community water organizations, in contrast with Chile (federated APR cooperatives/committees with legal cost-recovery/regulatory status since a 2017 Rural Sanitary Service Law), Ecuador (constitutionally recognized Juntas Administradoras de Agua Potable y Alcantarillado), and multiple Central American countries. In Mexico, 'legal arguments are invoked to deny recognition [to community organizations], such as municipal exclusivity for public service provision, the annual nature [of committee terms], or the inefficiency of rural water committees.' As of 2011, water coverage in Veracruz's rural areas was 73.5% (versus 94.0% in cities), and rural sewerage coverage was 73.9% (versus a national rural average of 82.9%). Of the 3 municipal administrative regions studied via CAEV's operating-office ratios, the northern zone had 14.7 rural systems per operating office, the central-Xalapa zone 9.8, the central-Córdoba zone 9.6, and the southern zone 5.5 -- reflecting highly uneven institutional capacity to support rural committees across the state. A field case in the Xalapa metropolitan zone documented a patronato with 850 registered household connections (as of 2003) that began operating informally in the 1930s, was only formally constituted as a civil association in 1970, and has continued without further federal, state, or municipal formal legal recognition since.

model_type: qualitative case-study analysis (semi-structured interviews, focus groups, and secondary administrative database review)
selection_bias: Moderate (purposively selected municipalities and rural committees within Veracruz's Xalapa metropolitan zone, not a representative sample of all Veracruz's ~2,000 OCSAS)
measurement_bias: Low-moderate (semi-structured interviews and focus groups triangulated with CAEV administrative inventory data and Conagua's national rural-committee database)
confounding: Not applicable (qualitative interpretive case-study analysis, not a causal design)

legal_measurement_quality: high (directly analyzes Veracruz's Ley 21/Ley 72 water and sanitation legal framework, the 1992/2013 constitutional Article 115 municipal-responsibility reform, and comparative Latin American legal-recognition frameworks for community water organizations)

citation: Akwataghibe N., Wegelin M., Postma L., Fajemisin W., Banda M.M., Khan F., Jurji Z., Toonen J. (2018). Exploring equity focus of the SHAWN WASH programme in Nigeria. Journal of Water, Sanitation and Hygiene for Development.
subnational_unit: 12 Local Government Areas (LGAs) across Bauchi, Jigawa, Benue, Katsina, Kaduna and Zamfara states
service_provider: UNICEF Sanitation, Hygiene and Water in Nigeria (SHAWN) II programme; community WASH Committees (WASHCOMs); LGA WASH departments
regulatory_model: Mixed-methods operational research (2,105-household survey, individual survey of physically disabled people, 62 in-depth interviews, 60 focus group discussions) assessing equity mainstreaming in the UNICEF SHAWN II WASH programme, examining needs-based and commitment-based LGA selection scoring criteria, community-level selection processes vulnerable to politicization via traditional-leader involvement, WASHCOM member-selection criteria (gender-balance quotas of 40-50%), the Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) no-subsidy approach with hardship-based support criteria for households unable to construct latrines themselves (due to lack or disability of a male household head), and political interference in water-point siting decisions producing skewed distribution
population: rural households in 12 LGAs across 6 SHAWN-programme Nigerian states
effect_measure: descriptive household-survey statistics (2,105 households, crude/adjusted logistic regression on WASH uptake) combined with qualitative thematic analysis of interviews/focus groups
effect_estimate: LGA selection used a weighted scoring system prioritizing underserved/hard-to-reach areas (highest scores for lowest accessibility during rains, greatest distance from state capital) plus sustainability-commitment criteria (signed chairperson letters, sensitization-meeting attendance, counterpart-funding timeframes) -- but stakeholders noted no clear mechanism ensured underserved LGAs unable to meet commitment criteria were still included. Community selection lacked a standardized process; most implementers described relying on traditional leaders to nominate qualifying communities, creating risk of politicization. WASHCOM formation guidelines required gender-balanced membership (7-13 members, 40-50% female), but this ratio was rarely achieved due to cultural/religious barriers ('the status of women is poor... many men will not allow their wives [in meetings]' -- key informant). Using the CLTS no-subsidy approach, approximately 21% of households in the household survey (HHS) had no latrine, 49% had unimproved latrines, and 29.7% had improved latrines (3.8% water seal). Support (financial or manual-construction assistance) was available from WASHCOMs for households unable to construct a latrine themselves, with eligibility criteria centered on lack or disability of a male household head. Significantly more of the poorest wealth quintiles (49%) reported satisfaction with the cost of water compared to the richest quintile (33%, p=0.000), explained by the fact that most communities did not collect user fees for water, with repair costs instead generated from WASHCOM-member or wealthier-resident contributions according to financial capacity. effect_estimate: Despite all three ASADAs holding the same formal ICAA delegation agreement and facing the same national regulatory framework, compliance and performance diverged sharply: Uvita (750 connections) and Matapalo (398 connections) reliably met ICAA water-quality standards (0 and 2.25 E. coli/100ml respectively) and complied with tariff, metering, and record-keeping rules, while Hatillo (174 connections, the smallest and poorest ASADA) operated in 'blatant disregard' of ICAA regulations (no water meters, tariffs below the ICAA-recommended rate, unchlorinated water averaging 218.25 E. coli/100ml) despite its board president being the most knowledgeable of all three about ICAA law and regulations -- 'the law is one thing, reality is another.' citation: Chowns E. (2015). Is Community Management an Efficient and Effective Model of Public Service Delivery? Lessons from the Rural Water Supply Sector in Malawi. Public Administration and Development 35(4):263-276.
subnational_unit: Four districts (two with high reported water-point functionality -- Mangochi, Thyolo; two with low -- Ntcheu, Chikhwawa), 24 randomly sampled VDCs

population: rural water-point users and Water Point Committee managers across 24 villages in 4 Malawian districts
sample_size: 679 water points; 276 users/managers surveyed; 26 key-informant interviews
effect_measure: descriptive mixed-methods statistics (household/manager survey, national database analysis, qualitative interview/blog coding)
effect_estimate: Community management has not generated the technical or financial benefits assumed by policy: true preventive maintenance is rare (most Managers only act on a water point once it breaks down), mean reported breakdown-repair duration was 136 days, and financial performance is far below expectations -- average savings held in Maintenance Funds were just 2% of the amount that should have been saved given household numbers, payment frequency, water-point age, and prior expenditure. Institutionally, District Water Offices report severe funding marginalization ('This month we got 59,000 [Malawi Kwacha] and we spent 35,000 on annual rental for our postal box') that leaves them unable to fulfil support, coordination, and supervision responsibilities, while national water-sector investment remains a tiny fraction of the government budget (1% in 2005/06, rising only to 3% in 2010/11, versus 16% each for education and health) and the water ministry has been progressively downgraded, losing ministerial status and being absorbed into the Ministry of Agriculture in the most recent government reshuffle. Decentralization has left districts with responsibilities but no resources, while the state and donors nonetheless continue to identify 'lack of community/local ownership' rather than the institutional/financial framework itself as the cause of poor performance, despite finding no statistical relationship between the existence of a (reportedly) active Water Point Committee and water-point functionality. The paper concludes that community management persists because it 'works' for the state and donors as a means of offloading long-term responsibility for public service provision, not because it is an efficient or effective delivery model.

citation: Subbaraman R., O'Brien J., Shitole T., Shitole S., Sawant K., Bloom D.E., Patil-Deshmukh A. (2012). Off the map: the health and social implications of being a non-notified slum in India. Environment and Urbanization 24(2):643-663.
subnational_unit: Kaula Bandar (KB), a non-notified slum on a wharf on Mumbai's eastern waterfront
service_provider: Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai (MCGM); Mumbai Port Trust (MbPT, central-government land-owning agency); Brihanmumbai Electricity Supply and Transport (BEST); informal private water vendors
regulatory_model: Mixed-methods four-year (2008-2012) community-based research collaboration (PUKAR-Harvard-NYU), comprising multiple quantitative surveys (959-4,063-household baseline/anthropometrics/water/diarrhoea surveys) and qualitative studies (focus-group discussions and semi-structured interviews), comparing Kaula Bandar's outcomes against India's National Family Health Survey-3 Mumbai-slum data, documenting the legal framework governing 'non-notified' slum status under a 1995 addendum to the Maharashtra Slum Areas Act 1971 (basic-amenity entitlement conditioned on pre-1995 residency proof), the No Objection Certificate (NOC) requirement from the central-government land-owning agency (MbPT) that blocks state extension of water/electricity/sanitation services onto central-government land, and documented criminalization of residents' self-help responses to service absence (police fines for informal water-tanker use and for open defecation)
population: residents of Kaula Bandar (10,000-12,000 people), a non-notified slum in Mumbai, India
sample_size: 1,701 households (2011 anthropometrics survey); 959-6,063 across various component studies
effect_measure: descriptive comparative statistics (Kaula Bandar vs. NFHS-3 Mumbai slums) plus qualitative interview/focus-group evidence
effect_estimate: Kaula Bandar's non-notified status legally precludes MCGM from extending piped water, sewer connections, formal electricity meters, or government-built toilets onto the land: only 0.1% of KB households have piped drinking water versus 99.7% of NFHS-3 Mumbai slums; residents instead purchase water from an informal vendor system charging 52-206 times the standard municipal tariff (6-16% of average monthly household income). Central-government land ownership (Mumbai Port Trust) compounds the exclusion: state agencies will not extend services onto MbPT land without an NOC, which MbPT withholds fearing extension of services would bolster residents' tenure claims -- creating a legal 'no-man's land' where no government authority takes responsibility for basic services. Open defecation and use of informal water tankers are actively criminalized: one resident reported being fined 1,800 rupees by police for bringing a water tanker into the community, and residents report routine arrests and fines (50-150 rupees each) for open defecation. Applications for a legitimate electricity connection were refused by BEST pending an NOC from MbPT, forcing residents into illegal, fire-risk-generating electricity theft. Lack of a 'below poverty line' ration card (linked to an inability to supply proof of residence given informal housing) blocks access to subsidized food and kerosene for 33% of surveyed households. Following a 2010 fire that destroyed ~9% of KB's homes, government disaster-compensation records showed only 4.6% of the estimated property loss was actually disbursed, compared with a notified Mumbai slum (Behrampada) that received a state rehabilitation package worth 37 times more per fire-affected household. KB residents also have no legal protection against forced eviction or right to rehabilitation upon displacement, unlike notified-slum residents.

Analyzes the Vivendi/Aguas del Aconquija v. Argentina ICSID investment-arbitration dispute arising from the Tucuman water concession (including the Tucuman Ombudsman's administrative dispute-resolution interventions and judicial evasion of a collective non-payment lawsuit); South Africa's shift from a political to a transactional water-tariff/disconnection regulatory framework (Free Basic Water Policy 2001, 2003 Strategic Framework credit-control code); and South African constitutional case law on disconnection due process (Residents of Bon Vista Mansions v. Southern Metropolitan Local Council; Manqele v. Durban Transitional Metropolitan Council) and cross-subsidy equality (Pretoria City Council v. Walker)

effect_measure: comparative doctrinal/qualitative case study (legal-case analysis, treaty/regulatory-document analysis, semi-structured interviews)
effect_estimate: In Argentina, mass consumer non-payment boycotts in Tucuman (in response to Vivendi/Aguas del Aconquija's tariff increases and water-quality problems) were channeled through the provincial Ombudsman, who issued resolutions discounting disputed bills and mounted an unprecedented (though ultimately unsuccessful) collective lawsuit on the boycotters' behalf; five consecutive judges each declined jurisdiction over the case, illustrating a structural gap in domestic dispute-resolution capacity. The concession was eventually terminated and Vivendi pursued a USD-denominated ICSID investment-arbitration claim against Argentina; substantive participatory gains for end-users were limited, though a legislative prohibition on disconnecting consumers using less than a basic minimum was achieved. In South Africa, the domestic regulatory framework shifted from a 'political' model (direct government-community engagement, extensive labour/consumer consultation rights under the Municipal Systems Act 2000) to a more 'transactional' model emphasizing tariff cost-recovery and private-sector-friendly credit control, formally softened only by non-binding 'soft law' instruments (the 2001 Free Basic Water Policy's 25-litres-per-person-per-day entitlement and the 2003 Strategic Framework's due-process/compassion principles for credit control). Constitutional litigation produced narrow, procedural rather than structural gains: Residents of Bon Vista Mansions held disconnection a prima facie breach of the constitutional right to water requiring due process (notice, opportunity to be heard, and reasonable procedures) before disconnection, but Manqele v Durban rejected a claim to enforce a specific minimum-water entitlement, and the Constitutional Court has more broadly declined to bind itself to international-law interpretations of a 'minimum core' of the right to water, remaining deferential to government policy choices on cross-subsidy design (Pretoria City Council v Walker, decided 5-4). The paper's central analytical finding is that 'global administrative law' in this domain is constituted through iterative interaction between formal legal processes and informal political modes (protest, negotiation, media) rather than through formal international legal doctrine alone, and that the relative capacity of end-users versus foreign water-service providers to switch between domestic and international levels of governance is sharply asymmetric, systematically favouring providers.

regulatory_model: Qualitative case study (key informant interviews, focus group discussions, household interviews, and document analysis) of institutional coordination among public, private, and community-based water supply schemes in Dar es Salaam, comparing one scheme from each of the three models. Documents the institutional framework for water supply (DAWASA, EWURA regulator, Wami-Ruvu Basin Water Office, municipal councils, Mtaa/sub-ward water committees), poor enforcement of regulatory instruments (most private providers unregistered, recognized only informally by residents), and comparative bureaucratic processing time for new water-connection applications across the three scheme types
population: households and water-supply-scheme actors (public, private, community-based) in Dar es Salaam
sample_size: three water supply schemes (one public, one private, one community-based), qualitative interviews/FGDs/household interviews
effect_measure: comparative case-study descriptive statistics (maximum processing days and actor counts per scheme type; no inferential exposure-comparator design)
effect_estimate: Time spent processing new water-connection applications varied sharply by scheme type: a maximum of 30 days in the public (DAWASA) scheme, 3 days in the private scheme, and 6 days in the community-based scheme, involving 5, 2, and 3 key actors respectively. The public scheme's delay was attributed to centralized processing at DAWASA headquarters (materials preparation, bank pay-slip documentation forwarded by the Area Office) despite nominal decentralization to area offices, while the community-based scheme's speed was attributed to all key actors being co-located within the same geographic service area. Most private service providers were found to be unregistered as formal service providers, recognized only informally by the residents they served, reflecting poor enforcement of the Water Supply and Sanitation Act 2019, EWURA Act, and other regulatory instruments.

measurement_bias: Low-moderate (multiple data-collection instruments -- document analysis, key informant interviews, household interviews, focus groups -- triangulated across the three schemes)
confounding: Not separately addressed
reporting_bias: Low-moderate (based on a doctoral thesis; explicit theoretical framing via coordination/institutional/network theory disclosed)
legal_measurement_quality: high (directly analyzes the Water Supply and Sanitation Act 2019, the EWURA Act No. 414 of 2001, the Water Resources Management Act No. 11 of 2009, and the National Water Policy 2002, and their differential enforcement across scheme types)
outcome_measurement_quality: moderate-high (specific processing-day and actor-count figures reported per scheme type in Table 1)

citation: Switzer D., Teodoro M.P. (2025). Public enterprise pricing as redistributive policy. Policy Studies Journal 53(2):365-387.
subnational_unit: 1,189 water utilities serving populations of 40,000+ nationwide
service_provider: 1,055 local-government-owned water utilities and 134 investor-owned (private) water utilities regulated by state Public Utilities Commissions
regulatory_model: Quantitative OLS regression analysis (n=1,183-1,189 US water utilities serving 40,000+ residents, 2019 residential water-price data combined with 2017 ACS income/demographic data) testing whether local income inequality (mean-to-median income ratio) correlates with the progressivity of water rate structures (unit price ratio, UPR), and whether this relationship differs between democratically-accountable local-government utilities (rates set by elected city councils/county commissioners/special district boards) and investor-owned utilities (rates set by state Public Utilities Commissions via a quasi-judicial cost-of-service process), adapting the Cukierman-Meltzer political-economy model of progressive taxation to public enterprise pricing
population: residential water customers of 1,189 US water utilities serving 40,000+ residents
sample_size: 1,183-1,189 water utilities (1,055 government-owned, 134 investor-owned), serving 183,314,934 people (~58% of US water utility customers)
effect_measure: OLS regression coefficient, unit price ratio (UPR) at 30,000 gallons monthly regressed on mean-to-median income ratio and utility ownership type, robust standard errors
effect_estimate: Model A (direct-effects only): a one-unit increase in the mean-to-median income-inequality ratio is associated with a 0.310 increase in the unit price ratio (more progressive pricing) (p=0.005); private/investor-owned ownership is associated with a -0.167 decrease in UPR relative to government ownership, i.e. more regressive pricing (p<0.001), holding population, median income, water scarcity, water source, and racial/ethnic composition constant. Model B adds a Private x Inequality interaction term (coefficient -0.209, p=0.387, not statistically significant), indicating no confirmed difference in the inequality-progressivity relationship between ownership types, though the interaction runs in the expected (weaker-for-private) direction. The inequality-progressivity relationship is positive and statistically significant across UPR calculated at monthly volumes from 12,000 to 60,000 gallons.
p_value: 0.005 (Model A, mean-to-median income ratio); <0.001 (Model A, private ownership); 0.387 (Model B, Private x Inequality interaction)
adjusted_or_unadjusted: adjusted (controls: log population, log median income, water scarcity (PDSI), groundwater source, purchased-water source, % Hispanic, % Black)
covariates: log population; log median income; water scarcity (reversed PDSI); groundwater source; purchased water source; % Hispanic; % Black
model_type: OLS regression with robust standard errors
risk_of_bias_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
selection_bias: Low-moderate (near-universe sample of all 1,189 US water utilities serving 40,000+ residents per EPA SDWIS, not a random or representative sample of all US utilities, but a defined and complete sampling frame for the study's stated population)
measurement_bias: Low (original hand-collected dataset of actual residential water rate schedules for each utility, cross-referenced against ACS 2017 5-year estimates for income/demographic covariates)
confounding: Explicitly addressed via multivariable OLS with 7 covariates including population, median income, water scarcity, water source type, and racial/ethnic composition; authors disclose cross-sectional design limits causal inference and cite the possibility of unobserved political factors correlated with both inequality and rate structures
