citation: Khadam N., Bukhtawer N., Iqbal Z., Qayyum H., Khan Z.F., Razzaq M., Idrees F. (2024). Gender inequality, water rights and policy implications: learning from the experience of experts working in water sector. Cogent Social Sciences 10(1):2334109.
subnational_unit: national and provincial (Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Sindh, Balochistan, Azad Jammu and Kashmir, Gilgit-Baltistan)
service_provider: provincial water authorities/commissions (e.g. Punjab Water Resource Commission) and local governments under Local Government Ordinance 2001
regulatory_model: Qualitative expert-panel-discussion study (six-stage Braun & Clarke thematic analysis of a virtual panel discussion with six key experts/stakeholders -- one male, five female -- with a minimum ten years' experience in law, policy, management, or gender/development in Pakistan's water sector) examining gender inequality in water rights and its policy implications. Documents the legal linkage between property/land ownership and formal water-connection eligibility (a documented connection is given to property owners, while the landless -- disproportionately women, since only 36 of 1000 women in Punjab own land -- are excluded and must travel to fetch water); the Punjab Water Act 2019's dissociation of water rights from land ownership (departing from the Easement Act 1882) as a gender-neutral but potentially beneficial reform; provincial water statutes (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Water Act 2020, Balochistan Water & Sanitation Authority Act 1989) that are silent on/gender-neutral toward women's representation; the Sindh Water Management Ordinance 2002, amended in 2018 to introduce a gender quota for women's participation in water governance bodies; AJK/GB water-governance laws that are gender-silent; and the Local Government Ordinance 2001's mandated council-seat reservations for women (33% Balochistan, 22% Khyber Pakhtunkhwa/Sindh, 15% Punjab), only ~19.6% of which were actually filled in the 2013/2015 elections
population: water-sector experts/stakeholders (law, policy, management, gender/development) in Pakistan, discussing women's and landless households' water access and rights
sample_size: 6 panel-discussion participants (1 male, 5 female)
effect_measure: qualitative thematic analysis (expert-panel discussion; no locatable quantitative effect estimate)
effect_estimate: Panellists reported that formal, documented water connections are given to property owners, while landless households -- who are disproportionately headed or represented by women, since only 36 of 1000 women in Punjab own land per ESCAP (2015) -- are 'automatically deprived of any water supply' and must travel far and queue in long lines to fetch water. The Punjab Water Act 2019 dissociated the legal right to water from land ownership (a departure from the Easement Act 1882), which panellists suggested could benefit women consumers, though the Act's key implementing body (the Punjab Water Resource Commission) carries no gender quota. Women's council-seat reservation targets under the Local Government Ordinance 2001 (ranging 15-33% by province) were only ~19.6% filled in practice (2013, 2015 elections).

model_type: qualitative expert-panel discussion (thematic analysis)
selection_bias: Moderate-high (purposive sample of 6 experts, disproportionately female by chance due to late male attrition; expert perceptions rather than direct study of affected households/landless women themselves)
measurement_bias: Low-moderate (video-recorded, transcribed panel discussion with rigorous six-stage Braun & Clarke thematic analysis, debriefing, and field notes)
confounding: Not applicable (qualitative thematic study)
attrition: Panel size reduced from an initially more balanced gender composition to 1 male/5 female due to last-minute non-availability of 2 male and 1 female invitee, disclosed by the authors as producing disproportionate gender representation by chance
reporting_bias: Moderate (explicit feminist/intersectionality theoretical framing disclosed; no pre-registration)

citation: Santos J.G., Ioris A.A.R. (2024). Water Conflicts and Socioterritorial Dynamics: The Hydrosocial Cycle After the São Francisco River Transposition Project in the Northeast of Brazil. Land 13(12):2032.
subnational_unit: São Francisco River basin, Northeast Brazil (Paraiba, Pernambuco, Ceara, Rio Grande do Norte states; rural villages in Monteiro, Sertania, Salgueiro municipalities)
service_provider: Ministry of Integration and Regional Development (MIDR, entrepreneurial agency); National Water Agency (ANA, regulatory agency); CODEVASF (federal operator); State Secretariats of Water Resources; state water companies (large users)
regulatory_model: Qualitative ethnographic study (48 semi-structured/oral-history interviews in 2019 across four rural resettlement villages, 12 follow-up interviews in 2024, plus semi-structured interviews with federal institutional actors -- MIDR, ANA, CODEVASF -- in 2024) of the São Francisco River Integration Project (PISF/'transposition project'), Brazil's largest water-infrastructure project, examining reterritorialization and access-to-water outcomes for the 845 families directly resettled into 18 rural villages built along the project route. Documents the formal governance structure (MIDR as implementing agency, ANA as regulator, CODEVASF as operator, state water companies classified as 'large users', rural villages/communities classified as 'small users'), a four-category environmental/resettlement compensation program (in-territory resettlement, self-resettlement, urban resettlement, rural collective resettlement), the exclusion of popular participation from the project's formal Management Board (only formal institutional actors participate, per interview with the General Coordinator of Contracts and Budgets), and the finding that proximity to the transposed water infrastructure itself does not guarantee resettled communities' access to or use of that water
population: rural families resettled/reterritorialized due to the PISF water-transposition project, and federal institutional actors responsible for the project
sample_size: 48 interviews (2019) + 12 follow-up interviews (2024) with resettled families, plus institutional-actor interviews (2024)
effect_measure: qualitative ethnographic case analysis (no locatable quantitative effect estimate)
effect_estimate: 845 families were directly affected and relocated to 18 rural villages built along the PISF route under a formal reterritorialization program; more families were indirectly affected but no clear statistics exist on the total number impacted. Despite the PISF's official discourse of universalizing water access for approximately 12 million inhabitants, and despite proximity to the transposed water infrastructure, resettled rural communities located directly in the PISF's surroundings are not guaranteed access to or use of the transposed waters. Popular participation was excluded from the project's formal Management Board, which comprises only formal institutional actors representing federal, state, and large-user (state water company/agribusiness) interests. Conflicts over land and water access deepened following implementation, reproducing historical patterns of water-source concentration by regional elites.

confounding: Not applicable (qualitative ethnographic case study)

citation: Wagle P. (2024). Water access disparity in Mumbai, India: Using spatial and structural attributes as formal conditionalities. Journal of Urban Affairs 46(4):831-844.
service_provider: Hydraulic (Water) Department of the Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai (MCGM)
regulatory_model: Qualitative study (formal/informal document analysis plus 64 multi-round semi-structured interviews with municipal engineers, academics/experts, political representatives, activists, and media persons, fieldwork 2019-2020) applying the theory of access (access-as-right and access-as-ability lenses) to formal water-connection entitlement disparity in Mumbai. Documents MCGM's two distinct water-connection application procedures for 'slum' vs. 'other-than-slum' dwellings, each carrying disparate formal service-level entitlements (45 LPCD standpost connection vs. 135 LPCD house-service connection), and the spatial/structural documentation conditionalities (Commencement Certificate, No-Objection-Certificate, Occupation/Building-Completion Certificate, Hydraulic Engineer 'Remarks' certifying internal water-distribution-system adequacy) that render informal, spatially/structurally 'deficient' dwellings ineligible for the full house-service connection and entitlement
population: residents of formal and informal ('slum') dwellings in Mumbai applying for MCGM water connections
sample_size: 64 semi-structured interviews across five professional categories
effect_measure: qualitative document/interview analysis of formal entitlement rules (no locatable quantitative effect estimate)
effect_estimate: Informal ('slum') dwellings are entitled only to a shared public standpost connection carrying a formal service level of 45 LPCD, while formal ('other-than-slum') dwellings are entitled to an individual house-service connection carrying a formal service level of 135 LPCD -- three times the entitlement. Approval of the full 135 LPCD entitlement requires satisfying a host of spatial and structural documentation conditionalities (CC, NOC, OC/BCC, Hydraulic Engineer Remarks certifying underground tank, overhead tank, pumping system, and piping network adequacy) that municipal engineers state informal dwellings cannot satisfy due to lack of open space and structural weakness, rendering them formally ineligible for house-service connections and full water entitlement. Standpost connections for slum dwellings additionally require documentary proof the dwelling existed before January 1, 2000, plus proof of the applicant's occupancy.

measurement_bias: Low (triangulates formal policy/legal document analysis -- including the two actual MCGM application forms -- with multi-round semi-structured interviews)
confounding: Not applicable (qualitative case study)
reporting_bias: Low (explicit theoretical framing via Ribot & Peluso's theory of access, disclosed as such; author states the paper does not assess the credibility/necessity of the conditionalities, only describes them)
legal_measurement_quality: high (directly analyzes and quotes MCGM's own application forms, BPAMS building-approval manual, and Water Charges Rules 2015)
outcome_measurement_quality: high (specific LPCD entitlement figures -- 45 vs. 135 -- and itemized documentation requirements drawn directly from MCGM's own formal policy instruments)

citation: Hofstetter M., Bolding A., Boelens R. (2023). Rooted Water Collectives in a Modernist and Neoliberal Imaginary: Threats and Perspectives for Rural Water Commons. Water 15(21):3736.
subnational_unit: Tshakuma and Ga-Moela, Limpopo Province, South Africa; Entlebuch, Kanton Luzern, Switzerland
legal_system: mixed (South Africa: common law/customary; Switzerland: civil law)
service_provider: user-owned/self-managed community water-collective committees; South African municipalities (Vhembe/Sekhukhune districts); Swiss cantonal department for agriculture and forestry (Kanton Luzern)
regulatory_model: Qualitative action-research/ethnographic case study (Rooted Water Collectives framework; semi-structured interviews with 28 department and 12 scheme officials, nine engineering consultants, 12 politicians, three academics, and 64 water users, across extended fieldwork/professional engagement 2017-2023) of three rural, user-owned/self-supply water collectives -- two in South Africa (Tshakuma, independently self-constructed; Ga-Moela, NGO/AfDB-funded participatory intervention) and one in Switzerland (Entlebuch, a 60-year-old cooperative). Documents how South Africa's Water Services Act 1997 and Municipal Systems Act 2000 rendered most CBO-supported community water schemes 'technically illegal' unless formally recognized as service providers through a public-tendering process, leaving these schemes operating in a legal grey zone dependent on municipal discretion/tolerance; and how Swiss cantonal subsidy systems and outsourcing of planning to private engineering consultants (following 1990s 'new public management' reforms) threaten collective schemes' operational autonomy and viability
population: rural households and communities served by user-owned/self-managed collective water schemes in South Africa and Switzerland
sample_size: 28 department/12 scheme officials, 9 engineering consultants, 12 politicians, 3 academics, 64 water users
effect_measure: qualitative comparative case analysis across three collectives (no locatable quantitative effect estimate)
effect_estimate: In South Africa, post-2000 legal reform (WSA 1997, MSA 2000) made the majority of CBO-supported water schemes 'technically illegal' as unlicensed service providers, though local governments in rural/poorer districts took a pragmatic approach and tolerated them; this leaves schemes' formal status contingent on municipal discretion rather than statutory right. The Tshakuma scheme (self-constructed, no external funding) grew from an initial 5 households to 113 committed households, providing reliable service through strong internal solidarity/contractual reciprocity; the Ga-Moela schemes (NGO/AfDB-funded participatory intervention) show weaker, uneven governance with unresolved operation/maintenance responsibility after municipal handover, and reproduce local power imbalances (preferential tap placement for the traditional chief's household, shortened pipe runs to tail-end households). The Swiss Entlebuch cooperative, though 60 years old and previously autonomous, was pressured by state subsidy conditions to merge with two other schemes into a larger, professionally managed unit, a move its committee successfully resisted.

model_type: qualitative comparative case study (Rooted Water Collectives / actor-oriented political-ecology framework)
selection_bias: Moderate (three purposively selected collectives across two countries, chosen for the main author's pre-existing professional access, not intended to be representative)
measurement_bias: Low (extensive multi-year embedded professional engagement -- action research -- plus 28+12+9+12+3+64 semi-structured interviews across all three cases)
confounding: Not applicable (qualitative case study)
reporting_bias: Low-moderate (explicit critical political-ecology theoretical framing -- modernist/neoliberal imaginary critique -- disclosed throughout)

outcome_measurement_quality: moderate-high (specific household counts -- 113 committed households in Tshakuma -- and detailed qualitative service-reliability/governance outcomes per case)

citation: Aigbavboa CO, Addo LY, Ebekozien A, Thwala WD, Arthur-Aidoo BM (2025). Appraising institutional management of urban water supply in Ghana: the role of the stakeholders. Journal of Facilities Management, 23(2), 269-288.
subnational_unit: Greater Accra Region (Accra East, Accra West, Tema)
service_provider: Ghana Water Company Limited (GWCL); district assemblies (permitting)
regulatory_model: Household connection to GWCL urban water supply requires the customer to submit a site plan, with an affidavit required 'in some situations'; the customer writes a letter to the district manager, after which a GWCL team conducts a site survey and issues a cost estimate (a process taking approximately two weeks), and the connection is completed only after payment is made. For individual connections the applicant is 'redirected to the assembly to obtain a permit' before GWCL connects them; for larger community needs, government agencies coordinate with GWCL to extend network lines, after which individual households go through the same procedure. Water quality is regulated through pre-distribution testing (acidity testing before and after treatment) under a drinking-water-management framework.
population: urban water service providers, regulators, government/non-governmental agencies, and domestic/commercial water users, Greater Accra, Ghana
sample_size: 19 qualitative key-informant interviewees; 521 survey respondents (of a 600 target sample, 86.83% response rate)
effect_measure: sequential exploratory mixed-methods design: qualitative thematic analysis of 19 key-informant interviews (urban water service providers, regulatory bodies, government agencies, NGOs) followed by a descriptive/exploratory-factor-analysis survey of 521 respondents (domestic/commercial water users, GWCL workers, regulators, NGOs, government agencies, private water distributors)
effect_estimate: Findings show that connecting a household to GWCL's urban water supply requires the customer to submit a site plan for the provision of water, with an affidavit added 'in some situations'; the customer writes a letter to the district manager, after which a GWCL team conducts a survey and issues a cost estimate (a process the study reports takes about two weeks), and the connection is completed only once payment is made (P5). For an individual household connection, the applicant is first 'redirected to the assembly to obtain a permit', after which GWCL completes the connection; for larger community-level needs, government agencies coordinate with GWCL to extend network lines to the community, after which individual households proceed through the same site-plan/permit/payment procedure. The quantitative survey identified 35 motivational factors for stakeholder engagement (top-ranked: 'growing water-based diseases such as guinea-worm need to be eradicated' and 'the health benefits of water', mean=3.52 each), 22 institutional factors for effective management (top-ranked: 'the policies for managing urban water supply need reforms', mean=3.19), and rated 'ensuring proper enforcement of laws' the lowest-ranked institutional-process item (mean=2.52 of 5), alongside 'there is fear and coercion to participate in the managing urban water supply' (mean=2.79). The study concludes that institutional processes, stakeholder engagement, and a regulatory framework with clearly enforced rules are jointly necessary for effective and inclusive urban water-supply management in Ghana.

citation: Murray A, Meyer F, Fourie E (2023). Workshopping Water Justice: linking struggles from the Cape Flats to the rest of the Continent. Globalisation, Societies and Education, 21(5), 705-719.
service_provider: City of Cape Town (CoCT), municipal water services department
regulatory_model: City of Cape Town water demand-management regime built around eligibility for 'indigent' status (a 'difficult process' in itself, required to receive the higher 350L/day free allocation via Water Management Devices rather than the standard 200L/day) combined with disconnection/flow-restriction enforcement: WMDs (2007-2021) dispensed a fixed daily volume before cutting off entirely; their 2021 replacement, a 'drip system', requires customers to self-manage usage to 15kL/month or face escalating punitive restriction (flow reduced to a 6kL/month trickle after three consecutive months over the cap, with the city manager empowered to unilaterally place a household on a prepaid meter after two such cycles), alongside a steeply regressive block tariff structure.
population: working-class residents of Cape Town informal settlements, backyard/frontyard dwellings and formal housing, organised through the African Water Commons Collective/Housing Assembly
tenure_status: mixed (formal housing, backyard/frontyard informal structures, informal settlements)
effect_measure: participatory-action-research/activist ethnography (decade of organising, 'revolutionary water workshops'/'water mapping' methodology) with documentary/policy analysis of municipal tariff and metering records
effect_estimate: Water Management Devices (installed 2007-2021) dispensed 200L/day at no charge before cutting off entirely, or 350L/day (87.5L per person per day for a modal working-class household of 4, but only 23L per person per day for the authors' documented modal household size of 15) if the household held 'indigent' status -- itself 'a difficult process' requiring registration and re-verification, bundled with a one-time arrears write-off after six months that was attractive to highly indebted households but also intensified state surveillance and criminalisation around 'indigent' status. WMDs were frequently installed improperly, without valid consent, or on the wrong property, and when they failed an 'unresponsive municipality' directed residents to sub-contractors and back again. Tariffs rose steeply and regressively: by 2017 the lowest consumption block (0-6kL, formerly free) had risen 556% while the top block saw a 104% increase, and more than two-thirds of WMDs were installed in working-class communities at the peak of the 2017-2018 Day Zero crisis. In April 2021 the City of Cape Town replaced WMDs with a 'drip system': households ('Customers', not 'residents') must self-manage usage below 15kL/month (500L/day average); exceeding this for three consecutive months triggers a flow-restricting disc limiting supply to a 6kL/month trickle (the FBW minimum) for 12 months, and after two such cycles the city manager can unilaterally place the household on a prepaid meter. The authors document that 'the bureaucratic process for indigent status and exclusionary eligibility requirements remains' under the new system, framing it as a continuation rather than resolution of water-access injustice, disproportionately affecting racialised, low-income and women-headed households who perform most water-related social-reproductive labour.

effect_estimate: In Ramirez v. Orange County Department of Health (1995), the court found OCDH had systematically failed to enforce sanitary code -- 22 of 36 permitted labor camps had unabated code violations across multiple growing seasons, including drinking-water contamination, flooded wells and unmonitored/untested well chlorine residual, which the county's own assistant commissioner for environmental health characterised as a 'respective condition' of migrant housing rather than a public-health hazard; despite documenting 515 code violations across the 1991-1992 seasons, the court found 'no real harm' once the plaintiffs had moved farms, leaving the underlying water/sanitation violations unremedied. In Gabriel v. Johnston's L.P. Gas Service (2016), triggered by a propane explosion in a converted, windowless farm-labor barrack that killed one worker and severely burned seven others, the court found 'no case law directly on point' regarding a propane supplier's duty to warn farmworker occupants (as opposed to the farm-owner 'customer') of safety hazards, and the state's Workers' Compensation Law exclusivity provision absorbed the farm owner's documented neglect of health/safety hazards into ordinary workplace risk, precluding tenant-landlord liability for seven of nine injured workers. citation: Grisaffi C, Leinster P, Sipuma R, Owako E, Parker A (2026). New definitions for good practice: Regulators as activists for urban road-transported sanitation in eastern and southern Africa. PLOS Water, 5(1), e0000385.
subnational_unit: national and local (utility/municipal) sanitation regulators, 5 East/Southern African countries
legal_system: mixed common law (former British colonial administrations, East/Southern Africa)
service_provider: national sanitation regulators (autonomous agencies/ministerial departments); utilities and municipalities acting as de-facto local regulators; formal and informal faecal-sludge emptying/transport service providers
regulatory_model: Multilayered national-and-local regulatory system governing safe emptying and transport of faecal sludge from onsite sanitation, in which the legal status of manual pit-latrine emptying varies by country (disallowed by some Kenyan county bylaws despite national guideline permission; legal if hygienic in Mozambique; legal with improved tools in Tanzania; at least semi-mechanised required in Uganda; legal and incorporated into national training in Zambia), with local regulators (utilities/municipalities) exercising informal discretionary enforcement -- issuing tacit amnesties, engaging informal/illegal manual emptiers rather than sanctioning them, and in some cases negotiating interim disposal sites involving other authorities 'turning a blind eye' -- to progressively formalise and scale safe service to low-income and informal areas.
population: national and local sanitation regulators, service providers (formal and informal manual pit emptiers), and low-income/informal urban households relying on road-transported (non-sewered) sanitation, East and Southern Africa
effect_measure: qualitative thematic analysis (19 semi-structured key-informant interviews with national/local regulators) combined with secondary-data review of prior WHO/ESAWAS transcripts (37 sources) and Delphi-study open-text responses (23 sources)
effect_estimate: All interviewed national and local regulators indicated that engaging informal manual pit emptiers -- rather than sanctioning or displacing them -- was essential to reaching universal access to safe sanitation in low-income areas, a finding the authors identify as novel for road-transported sanitation regulation globally. Local regulators described working 'in a legal grey zone,' negotiating interim disposal sites that required other authorities to informally tolerate non-compliant practice, and building relationships of trust with manual emptiers working 'illegally' to bring them 'on board' without 'crushing them.' One local regulator described the process: 'now we are at a stage where we can start to sanction... We've engaged them as much as we can... now let's start to identify what those penalties will be' -- illustrating a phased shift from tolerance/engagement toward eventual formal enforcement. National regulators described taking financial and political risks, including challenging International Financing Institutions and internal utility board resistance, to advance sector reform absent complete rules ('there was no regulatory framework and therefore everything was being done as pilot, or trial and error'). Regulators identified persistent gaps in requisite powers over household containment quality (pit latrine/septic tank design), overlapping and fragmented mandates with health, environment and labour departments enforcing sanctions on the same emptiers local regulators sought to engage, and inadequate resources and capacity across all five countries as barriers to consistent implementation. The authors frame utilities and municipalities acting in this capacity as de-facto 'local regulators' engaging in 'moral courage' -- a concept the study extends from regulatory-governance and business-ethics literature to the sanitation sector for the first time -- required to navigate incomplete rules, unclear mandates and limited resources while scaling access for the poorest and most stigmatised populations.

regulatory_model: Groundwater abstraction policies exist in municipal bye-laws in multiple HKH towns (cited: Quetta, Kabul, Dehradun, Haldwani) but are described as seldom enforced due to the political influence of informal water-tanker operators ('tanker mafia'); artificial low water pricing and absence of metering/differential pricing across most towns; institutional fragmentation across multiple departments/agencies responsible for water supply, management, and infrastructure maintenance, operating in silos with limited coordination.
population: Urban residents of HKH towns and cities, with explicit attention to socio-economically weaker/poor households who cannot afford premium-priced tanker water
sample_size: 8 cities with quantitative supply/demand data (Table 1); additional qualitative case discussion of ~10 further Indian Himalayan towns
effect_measure: Descriptive comparative synthesis (secondary-data compilation across 8 cities, no statistical contrast)
effect_estimate: Groundwater abstraction bye-laws exist in multiple towns (Quetta, Kabul, Dehradun, Haldwani) but are 'seldom followed,' with illegal/unregulated borewell proliferation attributed to weak enforcement and the political influence of informal tanker operators. Supply-demand gaps documented across 8 cities (Table 1): Kabul supplies only ~20% of population (15 Lpcd); Quetta has a 50% deficit (106 MLD supply vs. 170 MLD demand); Kathmandu Valley faces a 210 MLD shortfall (~70% gap); Shimla meets 84.2% of demand. Only the affluent can afford premium-priced tanker water (Kabul residents pay $0.36/unit for tanker deliveries); poor/socio-economically weaker areas experience recurring 'zero day' water cutoffs even where aggregate scarcity is not severe, reflecting inequitable distribution rather than pure physical scarcity. Absence of water metering and differential pricing across most towns is linked to inefficient use and poor demand management.
model_type: narrative policy synthesis (secondary-data/literature compilation plus author field observations from the HI-AWARE research consortium; no systematic-review search protocol)
study_design: narrative synthesis / policy-review case-study compilation across 8 Hindu Kush Himalaya cities, drawing on secondary literature, project reports, and author field observations

citation: Singh S, Hassan SMT, Hassan M, Bharti N (2020). "Urbanisation and water insecurity in the Hindu Kush Himalaya: Insights from Bangladesh, India, Nepal and Pakistan." Water Policy, 22(S1), 9-32.
subnational_unit: Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) regions of the 4 countries; cities/towns discussed include Rangamati, Baramula, Shimla, Mussoorie, Darjeeling, Kohima, Tansen, Kathmandu Valley (KUKL service area), Pokhara, Quetta, Rawalpindi, Mansehra, Karak
legal_system: mixed (civil law and common law across the 4 countries)
service_provider: Municipal/national water utilities (e.g., Kathmandu Upatyaka Khanepani Limited/KUKL, Ghana Water Company analogue in Pakistan's WASA, Darjeeling Municipality) plus private/informal water tanker vendors and household groundwater wells
regulatory_model: Departmental jurisdictional mandates limit spring/recharge-zone protection (e.g., the forest department in Darjeeling lacks mandate to extend artificial recharge outside protected areas); multi-party institutional coordination requirements (municipality, hill council, funding bodies) can delay and inflate the cost of water-augmentation projects; private tanker water markets operate with limited regulatory oversight, and pricing varies with distance, creating a financial burden that leads poorer households to restrict water quantity used.
population: Urban residents of Hindu Kush Himalaya towns and cities across Bangladesh, India, Nepal and Pakistan, with explicit attention to poorer households
sample_size: 13 cities with quantitative demand/supply data (Table 9); broader literature synthesis across the 4-country HKH region
effect_measure: Descriptive comparative synthesis (secondary-data compilation across 13 cities, no statistical contrast)
effect_estimate: Demand-supply deficits documented across 13 HKH towns (Table 9): KUKL service areas in Kathmandu Valley face a 178 MLD deficit (362 MLD demand vs. 184 MLD supply); Quetta a 64 MLD deficit; Rawalpindi a 59 MLD deficit. Governance and inter-departmental coordination failures identified as primarily responsible for the inability to manage groundwater in Darjeeling; despite clear departmental mandates, the forest department could not extend its mandate to artificial recharge outside protected areas, blocking spring rejuvenation region-wide. A Darjeeling water-augmentation project (lifting water from the Balasun river) stalled due to irreconcilable design/implementation/operation disagreements between the municipality, hill council, and World Bank, with project cost escalating from INR 400 million (2004 estimate) to INR 560 million by the time it restarted. Households buying water from private tankers face pricing that varies by distance, with documented financial implications restricting the quantity purchased by poorer households.

citation: Twum KO, Abubakari M (2020). "Drops in the city: the puzzle of water privatization and consumption deficiencies in urban Ghana." Water Policy, 22(3), 417-434.
subnational_unit: 4 major cities: Accra, Kumasi, Sekondi-Takoradi, Tamale
service_provider: Ghana Water Company Ltd (GWCL, public utility) alongside private water tanker operators, private borehole/well suppliers, and informal water retailers
regulatory_model: GWCL rationing schedule allocates water flows to different areas on selected days; boreholes require certification/approval from the Water Resources Commission; private water tanker and retail vendors operate with a weak/absent state regulatory environment (no enforced pricing controls), enabling exorbitant pricing; informal-settlement residents lack the legal documentation required to obtain formal household pipe connections, forcing reliance on private/informal water supply; no comprehensive private-sector water-supply policy or legislation currently governs private vendor operations.
population: Urban residents of Accra, Kumasi, Sekondi-Takoradi and Tamale, Ghana, including formal and informal/low-income neighborhoods
sample_size: 26 semi-structured interviews (12 urban residents across 4 cities, 4 Metropolitan Water and Sanitation Team officials per city, 2 Ghana Water Public Sector officials, 8 water-enterprise individuals) plus secondary data and GIS spatial analysis
effect_measure: Mixed-methods descriptive analysis (interview-derived themes plus secondary quantitative/GIS data, no statistical contrast)
effect_estimate: Only 30% of urban Ghanaians have access to piped water, which is itself often irregular; the remaining 70% rely on dug wells, springs, rainwater, boreholes or private vendors. GWCL supplies only 41% of the urban population despite an average daily output of 1,572,012 m3 against demand of 21,049,306 m3/day. In informal/poor neighborhoods, the lack of legal documentation for household pipe connections categorically bars residents from formal service, forcing reliance on private suppliers at exorbitant prices: $0.10/bucket from private well operators, $0.18/gallon from tanker operators, and $10-20 for untreated hand-dug-well water, versus much lower nominal costs for formally connected households. Private retailers themselves purchase bulk pipe water from GWCL at high prices (US$450) and pass costs to consumers. An average daily citywide supply deficit of an estimated 60 million gallons was documented (citing Peloso & Morinville 2014), with unequal distribution across neighborhoods and a documented decline in potable-water distribution rate from 76% (2008) to 59.8% (2012).
model_type: mixed-methods case study (semi-structured interviews, secondary data, GIS spatial mapping)
study_design: mixed-methods case study of water privatization and access inequality across 4 major Ghanaian cities, combining 26 semi-structured interviews with secondary data and GIS mapping

citation: Turley B, Caretta MA (2020). "Household Water Security: An Analysis of Water Affect in the Context of Hydraulic Fracturing in West Virginia, Appalachia." Water, 12(1), 147.
subnational_unit: Northwestern West Virginia, Appalachia (Marshall, Doddridge, Harrison, Kanawha, Marion, Monongalia, Ritchie, Tyler, Upshur, Wetzel counties)
service_provider: Household private groundwater wells (approximately two-thirds of research participants), with oil and gas companies' hired third-party contractors conducting mandated water testing
regulatory_model: West Virginia code 22-6A-18 (2013 Natural Gas Horizontal Well Control Act) establishes 'presumed liability': oil and gas companies are presumed liable for water-quality changes if a pre-drill and post-drill test show impact, changes occur within 6 months, and the water well is within 1500 feet of the gas well head; companies' own hired contractors conduct the mandated baseline and post-drill testing; oil and gas extraction is exempt from the federal Safe Drinking Water Act ('the Halliburton Loophole'), so industry-generated water-quality data are not made public; WV mandates setback distances of 250 feet from an existing water well/spring and 625 feet from an occupied building, based on government compromise rather than public-health science; USEPA does not regulate private water wells; WVDEP manages Underground Injection Control permits but a Natural Resources Defense Council report found it failed to enforce Safe Drinking Water Act UIC requirements (wastewater injected under expired permits, over half of wells abandoned unplugged).
population: Mineral owners, surface owners, and concerned citizens in 8 northwestern West Virginia counties near Marcellus/Utica shale hydraulic-fracturing development
sample_size: 30 semi-structured in-depth interviews (April-July 2018)
effect_measure: Qualitative thematic analysis (NVivo-coded, provisional coding) of 30 semi-structured interviews; no statistical contrast
effect_estimate: Residents' household groundwater security is undermined by uneven power relations built into the presumed-liability testing regime: water test results were frequently delayed by months, with residents in some cases learning only via FOIA requests that their water had already tested positive for contamination (e.g., E. coli, elevated arsenic and sodium) while continuing to drink it for months unknowingly. Presumed liability does not apply, and residents bear testing costs out-of-pocket, if the well is beyond the 1500-foot distance, if changes occur after 6 months, or if the company disputes causation (e.g., attributing arsenic to natural background levels). Non-disclosure agreements accompanying company buyouts or remediation suppress residents' ability to discuss confirmed contamination. Loss of usable water can render a home effectively unsellable, threatening residents' retirement savings and property value, while the company bears no equivalent financial risk. Residents report chronic anxiety, uncertainty, and mental stress that outweighs the economic benefits (jobs, tax revenue, mineral royalties) some also receive from extraction.
model_type: qualitative case study (feminist epistemology, purposive snowball sampling, semi-structured interviews, member checking)
study_design: qualitative case study of household groundwater security and water affect around hydraulic fracturing, based on 30 in-depth semi-structured interviews with mineral owners, surface owners, and concerned citizens in northwestern West Virginia
source_document: Turley & Caretta 2020, Water 12(1):147
section: 5. Water Affect in the Marcellus Shale (5.1 Power; 5.2 Emotional and Mental Stress)
exact_location: Section 3 (WV code 22-6A-18 presumed liability, setback distances, Safe Drinking Water Act exemption); Section 5.1 (delayed/incomplete industry-controlled water testing, NDAs, presumed-liability distance/time limits); Section 5.2 (property-value loss, financial and mental-health burdens)

citation: Dobbin KB (2020). "'Good Luck Fixing the Problem': Small Low-Income Community Participation in Collaborative Groundwater Governance and Implications for Drinking Water Source Protection." Society & Natural Resources, 33(12), 1468-1485.
subnational_unit: San Joaquin Valley, California (Tulare Lake and San Joaquin hydrologic regions)
service_provider: Small public water systems (cities, community services districts), privately-owned community water systems, and domestic well owners, all overseen by Groundwater Sustainability Agencies (GSAs) formed under California's Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA)
regulatory_model: SGMA (2014) requires local agencies in 127 high/medium-priority groundwater basins to form Groundwater Sustainability Agencies (GSAs) and develop Groundwater Sustainability Plans (GSPs) by 2020/2022; the statute lists 11 categories of beneficial users that must be involved, including Disadvantaged Communities (DACs, defined by median household income) and domestic well owners, but leaves the specific form of representation (voting member, non-voting member, advisory/stakeholder committee, or no formal relationship) to local GSA discretion; privately-owned water systems are legally barred from acting as a GSA independently and, per this study, none achieved formal representation despite technically available pathways; formal voting representation typically requires a financial contribution (e.g., one community's non-voting seat saved $8,000 versus a voting seat).
population: Small, low-income (Disadvantaged Community) drinking water stakeholders -- public water system staff/elected officials, residents/community leaders, and domestic well owners -- in California's San Joaquin Valley
sample_size: 27 semi-structured interviews with 35 individuals, representing 23 unique communities, conducted October 2018-May 2019
effect_measure: Qualitative thematic analysis (Dedoose-coded, structural and thematic coding of 1,066 coded excerpts) of 27 interviews; no statistical contrast
effect_estimate: Half (12 of 23) of represented communities had representatives actively involved in SGMA/GSA implementation; in no case did a privately-owned community water system or domestic-well community achieve formal GSA representation, though all types of local public water providers (including cities) lacked formal representation in at least one case. Financial barriers directly shaped participation: one community chose a non-voting GSA role over a voting one to save $8,000. Interviewees with advisory/stakeholder (non-voting) positions repeatedly described having 'voice but not vote,' and even those with formal voting seats often felt uninfluential ('majority rules'). Transparency failures were common: non-Brown-Act-compliant meetings, last-minute cancellations, and one community's first notification about SGMA arriving in 2018, three years after the law took effect. Across nearly all interviews, drinking-water/water-quality considerations were reported as absent or a minimal part of GSA deliberations and Groundwater Sustainability Plan (GSP) development, and 25% of interviewees explicitly expected SGMA's net effect on their community to be negative (new fees/costs for already-unaffordable water, moratoria/reductions risking existing wells running dry) rather than a source-water-protection benefit.
model_type: qualitative case study (semi-structured interviews, purposive plus snowball sampling, constant comparative coding)
study_design: qualitative case study of small low-income community participation in collaborative groundwater governance under California's Sustainable Groundwater Management Act, based on 27 semi-structured interviews with 35 individuals across 23 San Joaquin Valley communities
source_document: Dobbin 2020, Society & Natural Resources 33(12):1468-1485
section: Community Participation in SGMA Implementation; Challenges (Lack of Access; Lack of Influence); Implications for Source Water Protection and Rural Drinking Water Provision
exact_location: Table 2 (types and prevalence of formal relationship between small DACs and overlying GSAs); Challenges section (financial, technical, and institutional barriers to representation); Implications section (absence of drinking-water considerations in GSP development)

Documents a genuine legal-administrative participation regime: SGMA statutorily lists Disadvantaged Communities and domestic well owners among 11 mandatory beneficial-user categories, but leaves the form of representation to GSA discretion, resulting in privately-owned water systems and domestic-well communities never achieving formal voting representation; financial cost of voting seats, technical/staff capacity disparities, and transparency failures (non-Brown-Act-compliant meetings, delayed notification) compound exclusion; drinking-water needs are largely unaddressed in resulting Groundwater Sustainability Plans. record_id RC85926098F35.

citation: Singh S, Shrestha K, Hamal M, Prakash A (2020). "Perform or wither: role of water users' associations in municipalities of Nepal." Water Policy, 22(S1), 90-106.
service_provider: Water Users' Associations (WUAs) / Drinking Water Users' Associations (DWUAs) operating under Nepal Water Supply Corporation and municipal oversight
regulatory_model: Nepal's water-supply governance is set by the Constitution of Nepal 2015 (Art 25(4), right to clean drinking water), the Essential Commodity Protection Act 1955, the Water Resource Act 1992 and Water Resource Regulation 1993 (establishing water use priorities and WUA formation), the Drinking Water Regulation 1998 (governing DWUA/WUA registration and operation), the Nepal Water Supply Corporation Act 1989, and the Local Self Governance Act 1999 (devolving service delivery to local bodies); WUAs are community-elected committees legally responsible for connection approval, tariff-setting, and system maintenance, with limited external accountability mechanisms.
population: Households in Damauli and Tansen municipalities served (or seeking to be served) by local Water Users' Associations
sample_size: 350-household survey (208 Damauli, 142 Tansen) plus focus group discussions
effect_measure: Descriptive survey statistics (household survey, N=350) plus qualitative FGD themes; no statistical contrast
effect_estimate: New household tap connections cost NPR 50,000 (~USD 440) through the standard WUA queue, with waiting times reported up to 11 years; households able to pay double (NPR 100,000) could obtain faster connection, documenting a two-tier informal-payment access mechanism. WUA committees were found to collude with private repair agencies (kickback arrangements) and to be politically captured -- the same individuals were repeatedly re-elected with little accountability to the wider membership. Taps are registered only in the name of the male household head, structurally excluding women from formal water rights even though women perform 6-7 hours/day of water collection during the dry season when piped supply fails. Households unable to access piped supply relied on private tanker water at approximately Rs 357 (~USD 3) per 1,000 litres. Spring-water pricing by WUAs rose inequitably from NPR 20 to NPR 80 per 6,000 litres. Larger, better-resourced WUAs were reported to 'lobby to buy' water sources away from smaller, less powerful WUA committees, compounding inter-community inequity.
model_type: mixed-methods household survey and focus group discussions
study_design: mixed-methods study (350-household survey across two municipalities plus focus group discussions) of the role, performance, and accountability of Water Users' Associations in municipal Nepal
source_document: Singh, Shrestha, Hamal & Prakash 2020, Water Policy 22(S1):90-106
section: Results; Discussion (WUA governance, connection costs, gender exclusion, tanker/spring pricing)
exact_location: Household survey results and FGD findings on connection costs/waiting times, WUA committee accountability and corruption, gendered tap registration, and tanker/spring water pricing
extraction_note: Extracted from full-text PDF (retrieved via Google Drive inbox). Documents a genuine legal-administrative access regime under Nepal's Water Resource Act 1992/Regulation 1993 and Drinking Water Regulation 1998: WUA-administered connection queues with multi-year waits, an informal pay-to-jump-queue mechanism, WUA committee corruption and political capture, gendered exclusion via male-only tap registration, and inequitable WUA pricing/inter-committee water-source competition. record_id R55F012C376B7.

citation: Sarrazin C, Gautier E, Hollé A, Grancher D, de Bélizal E, Hadmoko DS (2019). "Resilience of socio-ecological systems in volcano risk-prone areas, but how much longer? Assessment of adaptive water governance in Merapi volcano, Central Java, Indonesia." GeoJournal, 84, 183-213.
subnational_unit: Merapi volcano southern slopes, Central Java (7 villages/dusun)
service_provider: Water Users Associations (WUA) and WUA Federations (post-Turnover Program), alongside informal Ulu-Ulu customary water officials and government agencies (Ministry of Public Works, Ministry of Agriculture & Environment, regional Perusahaan Daerah Air Minum)
regulatory_model: Indonesia's 1987 irrigation reforms and the 1998/1999 decentralization framework (under the Indonesian Local Autonomy Act 1972 lineage) established the 'Turnover Program,' transferring irrigation governance from customary Ulu-Ulu rights-holders to formal Water Users Associations (WUA) and WUA Federations; resulting institutional pluralism/fragmentation spans the Ministry of Public Works, the Ministry of Agriculture & Environment, regional water agencies (Perusahaan Daerah Air Minum), the Irrigation Committee, and informal Ulu-Ulu customary authorities, producing documented coordination failures including an undelivered 2013 government subvention payment owed to WUAs.
population: Households and community stakeholders in 7 villages/dusun on Merapi volcano's southern slopes, Central Java
sample_size: 73 stakeholder interviews, including 42 household-level interviews (22 farmers, 10 fish farmers, 10 non-agricultural villagers); 1-month fieldwork in 2013
effect_measure: Qualitative thematic analysis of 73 stakeholder interviews (42 household-level); no statistical contrast
effect_estimate: The 'Turnover Program' formally shifted irrigation governance from customary Ulu-Ulu rights-holders to WUAs/WUA Federations, but institutional pluralism across the Ministry of Public Works, Ministry of Agriculture & Environment, regional water agencies, the Irrigation Committee, and residual informal Ulu-Ulu authority produced coordination failures, including a documented 2013 case where agreed government subvention payments to WUAs were never transferred. Following the 2010 Merapi eruption, lahar (volcanic mudflow) damage to sabo-dams and irrigation canals caused acute drinking-water and irrigation-water crises; government emergency water-tank distribution during this period was reported as unequal across villages, and communities relied on informal Gotong Royong mutual-aid labor -- outside any formal legal/institutional channel -- to repair damaged irrigation canals themselves.
model_type: mixed-methods stakeholder interview study (semi-structured interviews, single-month fieldwork)
study_design: mixed-methods case study (73 stakeholder interviews, including 42 household-level) of adaptive water governance and post-eruption institutional resilience on Merapi volcano's southern slopes
source_document: Sarrazin, Gautier, Hollé, Grancher, de Bélizal & Hadmoko 2019, GeoJournal 84:183-213
section: Results (Turnover Program and institutional pluralism; post-eruption water crisis and emergency response)
exact_location: Sections documenting the Turnover Program's transfer of irrigation governance from Ulu-Ulu to WUAs, institutional fragmentation among government agencies, the undelivered 2013 subvention case, and post-2010-eruption lahar damage/emergency water distribution/Gotong Royong canal repair

Documents genuine Indonesian legal-institutional content: the Turnover Program's formal transfer of irrigation governance from customary Ulu-Ulu authority to WUAs/WUA Federations under the 1987 reform and 1998/1999 decentralization framework, cross-agency institutional pluralism causing an undelivered 2013 WUA subvention, and household/community-level post-disaster water-access disruption and informal (Gotong Royong) versus formal government emergency response. record_id REB0B1F68FC00.

citation: Nyamwanza AM (2018). "Local institutional adaptation for sustainable water management under increasing climatic variability and change: A case in the mid-Zambezi Valley, Zimbabwe." International Journal of Climate Change Strategies and Management, 10(3), 453-471.
subnational_unit: Mbire District, Mashonaland Central Province (mid-Zambezi Valley)
service_provider: Rural District Council (RDC), Environmental Management Agency (EMA), traditional authorities (chiefs, headmen, village heads, spirit mediums), the Ministry of Transport, Communication and Infrastructural Development's District Development Fund (DDF) unit, and elected Borehole Water Committees (BWCs)
regulatory_model: Zimbabwe's water governance rests on the Water Act 1998 and the Zimbabwe National Water Authority (ZINWA) Act 1998, which vest water ownership in the President and establish Catchment Councils (CCs) and Sub-Catchment Councils (SCCs) as the formal water-planning/permitting bodies; the Environmental Management Act 2002 (administered by EMA) governs natural-resource and pollution regulation including a streambank-cultivation ban; the Rural District Councils Act 1996 empowers RDCs to formulate local by-laws; the Public Health Act 2002 covers water-quality/sanitation. In Mbire District, however, CCs, SCCs and ZINWA were found to be functionally absent -- over 90% of surveyed residents had no knowledge of CCs/SCCs -- leaving the RDC, EMA, traditional authorities, and community-level BWCs as the institutions actually governing local water access.
population: Rural households and communities across 17 wards of Mbire District, Zimbabwe
sample_size: 34 semi-structured interviews, 3 community workshops, plus key informant interviews with national- and local-level officials and documentary review
effect_measure: Qualitative thematic analysis of 34 semi-structured interviews and 3 community workshops; descriptive survey statistics on institutional awareness and water-availability perceptions; no statistical contrast
effect_estimate: Over 90% of interviewed residents had no knowledge of the responsibilities, operations or activities of the formally mandated Catchment Councils and Sub-Catchment Councils, and although most had heard of ZINWA (mainly via media coverage of urban activities), none had ever interacted with a ZINWA official; slightly over 60% of respondents reported that water availability for agricultural and domestic use had become scarcer over the preceding five years. The RDC's contentious enforcement of the national streambank-cultivation regulation (prohibiting cultivation within 30m of a public stream) produced open animosity with residents dependent on riverbank farming for dry-season livelihoods, including reported death threats against EMA officers; the RDC and traditional leadership negotiated a local modification permitting hoe-only riverbank cultivation, but EMA did not fully accept this accommodation, producing ongoing inter-institutional conflict. Borehole access was severely strained: with the exception of one ward, every ward exceeded the government's recommended maximum of 250 persons (25 families) per borehole, with the worst-affected ward (Masoka, Ward 11) reporting over 2,000 persons per functioning borehole, a situation worsened by the collapse of donor funding for the DDF drilling/maintenance unit after 2000 and periodic flood-related borehole contamination.
model_type: qualitative case study (semi-structured interviews, community workshops, key informant interviews, documentary review)
study_design: qualitative case study of local water-related institutional adaptation to climate-related challenges in Mbire District, Zimbabwe, based on 34 semi-structured interviews, 3 community workshops, key informant interviews, and documentary review
source_document: Nyamwanza 2018, International Journal of Climate Change Strategies and Management 10(3):453-471

Documents a genuine legal-institutional access regime: statutorily mandated Catchment/Sub-Catchment Councils and ZINWA are functionally absent in this rural district, leaving RDC by-laws, EMA enforcement, traditional authority, and community-run Borehole Water Committees as the operative (and sometimes conflicting) governance layers; RDC/traditional-authority negotiated accommodation of a national streambank-cultivation ban illustrates real regulatory discretion and local modification in practice. record_id RACFFE4F7F72C.

citation: Bartels LE, Bruns A, Alba R (2018). "The production of uneven access to land and water in peri-urban spaces: de facto privatisation in greater Accra." Local Environment, 23(12), 1172-1189.
subnational_unit: Oduman (Ga West Municipality) and Pantang (La Nkwantanang-Madina Municipality), Greater Accra Metropolitan Area (GAMA)
service_provider: Ghana Water Company Limited (GWCL, urban mandate), Metropolitan/Municipal/District Assemblies and Community Water and Sanitation Agency (rural/small-town mandate), private water vendors (mobile tankers and neighbourhood groundwater sellers/retailers), and customary traditional authorities (chiefs, family heads) governing land
regulatory_model: Ghana's Water Resources Commission Act 1996 vests all water resources in the President in trust for the people and requires extraction permits/registration under the Water Use Regulations 2001 (L.I. 1692); GWCL holds the statutory urban water-supply mandate, MMDAs the rural/small-town mandate, with CWSA facilitating rural provision. Land is governed by legal pluralism: customary stool/skin/family land (78% of GAMA land) is held in allodial title by traditional authorities as fiduciary custodians for the landowning group, alongside statutory registration under the Title Registration Act 1986; the Constitution of Ghana 1996 bars freehold interests in stool land, permitting only leasehold registration. In practice, groundwater extraction in the case-study sites occurs almost entirely without the legally required permits/registration, and land management is frequently privatised by chiefs/family heads and other landowning-group members who retain land-sale proceeds personally rather than for the landowning group.
population: Households in the original villages and 'new site' peri-urban settlements of Oduman and Pantang, Greater Accra
sample_size: 62 semi-structured household interviews (1-2 hours each, snowball sampling), plus transect walks, week-long household photo diaries, and interviews with private water providers, traditional authorities, elders, youth-organisation members, and landowner associations
effect_measure: Qualitative thematic analysis (MAXQDA-coded transcripts) of 62 household interviews plus triangulating transect walks, photo diaries and expert interviews; no statistical contrast
effect_estimate: Only about half of the urban GAMA population has access to piped water, with private water providers filling the gap; residents pay 3-20 times higher prices for private-vendor water than the official GWCL rate, with further price variation between tanker-retail and groundwater-seller sources depending on income and perceived quality. Groundwater extraction is de facto privately controlled by landowners without the legally required Water Use Regulations 2001 permit/registration. In the land domain, an unresolved 20-year chieftaincy dispute in Oduman (beginning with a 1998 destoolment) created an authority vacuum in which family elders, youth, and the chief's rivals sold customary land multiple times to different buyers; residents responded by immediately erecting physical structures, posting 'not for sale' signs, hiring land guards/caretakers, or resorting to court to maintain access, since formal land titles played only a minor role (most residents had none, and registration was frequently impossible because the underlying stool land itself was unregistered). Nearly all households developing land in the 'new sites' had to pay an informal, negotiable 'digging fee'/asafo money to the village youth before construction could begin, with obstruction of construction activities for non-payment.

study_design: mixed-methods case study of de facto privatisation and uneven access to land and water in two peri-urban localities (Oduman and Pantang) of the Greater Accra Metropolitan Area, Ghana, based on 62 household interviews plus triangulating qualitative methods

citation: Nastar M, Abbas S, Aponte Rivero C, Jenkins S, Kooy M (2018). "The emancipatory promise of participatory water governance for the urban poor: Reflections on the transition management approach in the cities of Dodowa, Ghana and Arusha, Tanzania." African Studies, 77(4), 504-525.
subnational_unit: Dodowa (Shai-Osudoku District, Greater Accra Region), Ghana; Arusha, Tanzania
service_provider: Ghana Water Company Limited (GWCL, urban piped supply), Community Water and Sanitation Agency (CWSA, rural/small-town coordination), District Assembly (DA)-supported WATSAN committees, and traditional community leaders (Dodowa); Arusha Urban Water Supply and Sewerage Authority (AUWSA), Pangani Basin Water Board (PBWB), Arusha City Council (ACC), and informal Balozi/street-chair structures (Arusha)
regulatory_model: In Ghana, the Community Water and Sanitation Agency Act assigns CWSA responsibility for coordinating participatory rural/small-town water management and supporting District Assembly-established WATSAN committees that manage groundwater boreholes, while GWCL holds the statutory urban piped-supply mandate; new tank connections require a GWCL site inspection and application process. In Tanzania, the Water Resource Management Act assigns the Pangani Basin Water Board regulatory authority over groundwater drilling/permitting, but a lack of monitoring budget has left a growing number of boreholes unregistered; the Arusha City Council's land-permitting authority for the expanding urban periphery has been used to issue permits in designated groundwater recharge areas, a practice a National Environment Management Council official confirmed is illegal under the Water Resource Management Act.
population: Households in low-income and informal peri-urban/urban settlements of Dodowa, Ghana (9 suburbs) and Arusha, Tanzania (6 wards)
sample_size: 104 household interviews in Dodowa (42 in Dec 2015, 72 in Feb/Mar 2016); 56 household interviews plus 120 unstructured interviews at 70 water points in Arusha (Nov 2015-Jan 2016); plus document analysis and interviews with government/NGO organizational actors
effect_measure: Qualitative thematic analysis (coded interview data) of 104 Dodowa household interviews, 56 Arusha household interviews, and 120 Arusha water-point interviews, triangulated with document analysis; no statistical contrast
effect_estimate: In Dodowa, over half of residents rely on GWCL piped water delivered via household connections or nearby water tanks requiring an application/inspection process and connection fee; residents without their own connection buy water from tank owners at roughly 10 times the per-unit GWCL tariff (approx. 3.5 pesewas/20L for connection owners vs. 30-70 pesewas/20L from tank resellers), with no price monitoring by GWCL. Of nine studied suburbs, only three had an established WATSAN committee to manage boreholes, and even there many households were unaware of the committee's existence or membership; renters and non-native residents (e.g. the respondent Afua) reported feeling they had no standing to raise complaints about water governance because they did not own land. In Arusha, AUWSA's piped network serves only 44% of the population and is concentrated in the city centre; the Pangani Basin Water Board lacks the operational budget to identify or monitor a growing number of unregistered boreholes, and the Arusha City Council has issued land permits for development in designated groundwater recharge areas, confirmed by a National Environment Management Council official to be illegal under the Water Resource Management Act. Both cities show household-level access to water and to community water governance shaped by informal social hierarchies -- traditional chiefs/elder committees/royal families and Balozi/street chairs/landlords -- with tenure status, kinship ties, and land ownership determining who is heard and who is structurally excluded from decision-making and resource access.

study_design: mixed-methods comparative case study of power dynamics in participatory groundwater governance for the urban poor in Dodowa, Ghana and Arusha, Tanzania, based on document analysis and 104+56 household interviews plus 120 water-point interviews

citation: Romano ST (2017). "Democratic Decentralization and Community-Based Water Governance: The Case of Nicaragua's Water Committees (CAPS)." (qualitative case study of the legal recognition and organic empowerment of rural water committees in Nicaragua).
subnational_unit: Rural communities served by community-based water and sanitation committees (CAPS)
service_provider: Community-based Potable Water and Sanitation Committees (CAPS)
regulatory_model: Nicaragua's Special Law of Potable Water and Sanitation Committees (Law 722, 2010) formally recognized over 5,000 previously unrecognized CAPS serving more than 1 million rural residents, granting them legal standing within the national water-governance framework. The prior General Water Law (Law 620, 2007) had excluded CAPS from formal recognition. Even after Law 722, CAPS individually lack personeria juridica (legal personality) unless separately registered, which prevents them from legally receiving title to constructed water systems from NGOs/government agencies.
population: Rural water committees (CAPS) and their member households; NGO, multilateral, and government staff involved in rural water governance
sample_size: 18 semi-structured interviews with rural water committees plus interviews with NGO/multilateral/government staff, 12 months of fieldwork 2007-2010, plus 2014 follow-up
effect_measure: Qualitative thematic analysis of 18 semi-structured committee interviews plus NGO/multilateral/government stakeholder interviews across 12 months of fieldwork (2007-2010) and a 2014 follow-up; no statistical contrast
effect_estimate: Law 722 (2010) formally recognized over 5,000 previously unrecognized CAPS serving more than 1 million rural residents, a major shift from the exclusionary General Water Law (Law 620, 2007). Despite this recognition, individual CAPS still generally lack personeria juridica (legal personality), which prevents them from legally receiving title to water systems constructed on their behalf. CAPS set and collect user fees ranging from $0.23 to $2.85 per household per month, and in practice negotiate informal, unenforced exceptions to shutoff rules for seasonal-labor households unable to pay during the agricultural off-season. CAPS also engage in legally ambiguous negotiation of land and water-source access with private landowners, since formal easement or expropriation mechanisms are often unavailable or inaccessible to them, reflecting an 'organic empowerment' process in which CAPS built de facto governance authority and community legitimacy well before -- and continuing to exceed -- their formal legal recognition.

subnational_unit: Groot Marico catchment, North West Province
service_provider: Water User Association (WUA) established under the National Water Act 1998
regulatory_model: South Africa's National Water Act 1998 defines and establishes guidelines for Water User Associations (WUAs) as the local collaborative-governance vehicle intended to redress apartheid-era water-access inequality by bringing water users of all types into a common local management structure. The NWA's 'existing lawful use' provision ties commercial-farmer water entitlements to land ownership and water use as of the 1996-1998 baseline period, which in practice continues to advantage the white minority of commercial irrigation farmers who held land and registered use at that time, despite the Act's stated intent to progressively separate water rights from land ownership.
population: Commercial farmers, emerging (Black smallholder) farmers, and local community members in the Groot Marico catchment
sample_size: 48 semi-structured and focus-group interviews with commercial farmers, emerging farmers, and local community members, plus document analysis, fieldwork 2011 and 2015
effect_measure: Qualitative thematic analysis of 48 semi-structured and focus-group interviews plus document analysis of WUA-establishment records, across fieldwork in 2011 and 2015; no statistical contrast
effect_estimate: The National Water Act 1998's 'existing lawful use' provision, tying commercial-farmer water entitlements to land ownership and use as of the 1996-1998 baseline, continued to advantage the white minority of commercial irrigation farmers despite the NWA's stated intent to progressively separate water rights from land ownership. A documented WUA-establishment meeting saw Black rural community members and emerging farmers functionally excluded from meaningful participation through short notice, an inaccessible venue, and English-only proceedings, resulting in commercial farmers dominating the vote on WUA leadership and the adoption of a pre-drafted constitution that emerging farmers and community members had no substantive opportunity to shape. Emerging farmers reported that even after WUA establishment, the association's governance structure continued to reflect and reproduce pre-existing power asymmetries rather than functioning as the equitable collaborative-governance vehicle the NWA envisioned.

citation: Kim E (2014). "Conceptual practice of 'rural wellbeing' in Uzbekistan: Contradictions and implications for gender equality." Rural Society 23(3):243-256.
service_provider: Water User Association (WUA), municipal pump managers, state water agencies, foreign-funded international development project
regulatory_model: The Uzbek government institutionalized Water User Associations (WUA) to organize village-level water management following the post-1991 decollectivization of former Soviet collective/state farms; by 1994 individual household peasant-farm land plots (approx. 0.13 hectares) were formalized with permanent and inheritable access rights; private farmers (all male in the study village) hold long-term lease contracts requiring annual submission of cotton and a set wheat quota to the state at state-determined prices, with fines for shortfall. A foreign-funded participatory water-management development project (2008 onward) worked to strengthen the WUA's institutional organization, using 'community mobilisation' criteria (public visibility/authority, community respect, free time) for selecting local 'mobilisers' that discursively and structurally excluded women, despite women constituting the majority of household farmers.
population: Women peasant heads-of-household farmers (majority of Chaika's household farmers); private male farmers; WUA staff; municipal pump managers; state water agency representatives; international development project staff
sample_size: 40 in-depth interviews with women peasants; 8 project staff and 65 water-management stakeholders interviewed; participant observation; ~400 institutional documents analyzed (fieldwork spring/summer 2011)
effect_measure: Qualitative institutional-ethnographic thematic analysis (in-depth interviews, participant observation, and institutional text analysis); no statistical contrast
effect_estimate: Women peasant farmers, though the majority of Chaika's household farmers and heads of households, were structurally excluded from a foreign-funded participatory WUA water-management project: the criteria for selecting 'mobilisers' (unquestioned public authority/respect, free time) discursively assumed only men could meet them, and no women were selected despite meeting the technical-knowledge criterion. Interviewed women reported extensive unrecognized, unpaid labor negotiating access to scarce irrigation water -- physically walking up to several kilometers to check canal flow, queuing with other smallholders, and developing informal monitoring strategies (stopping passing cars, watching for village council members) to anticipate water arrival -- while private male farmers had unproblematic access to irrigation water and other project services. Women's self-organized, independent water-user groups closely resembling the project's own 'community mobilisation' goals were never recognized or incorporated by project staff. More than 80% of these women's household subsistence relied on garden/field produce dependent on this irrigation access.
model_type: institutional ethnography (in-depth interviews, participant observation, institutional text analysis)
study_design: qualitative institutional ethnographic case study (40 in-depth interviews with women peasant farmers plus 65 additional stakeholder interviews, participant observation, and ~400-document institutional text analysis) of gendered exclusion from a participatory Water User Association project in rural Uzbekistan

citation: Selfa T, Bain C, Moreno R (2014). "Depoliticizing land and water ''grabs'' in Colombia: the limits of Bonsucro certification for enhancing sustainable biofuel practices." Agriculture and Human Values 31:455-468.
subnational_unit: Valle del Cauca (Palmira, Candelaria, Cerrito, Pradera municipalities)
service_provider: Cauca Valley Corporation (CVC, regional water/environmental authority), sugarcane industry associations (Asocana, Procana), Bonsucro (private multi-stakeholder certification initiative)
regulatory_model: Colombia's water-concession regulatory regime (Decree 1541/78, Agreement 042/2010) governs surface- and groundwater use; the Cauca Valley Corporation (CVC), created in the 1950s and reconstituted as a regional environmental authority under 1993 Law 99, administers water concessions and quality regulation but is described by multiple interviewees as captured by the sugar industry, with water-use restrictions nominally existing but not enforced. The sugar industry holds 64% of surface-water and 88% of underground-water concessions in the Valle del Cauca (versus 26%/2% for household use) at lower rates than other users. Bonsucro's 'Principle 1: Obey the law' land-rights standard (requiring compliance with national land-tenure law and ILO Convention 169) and 'Principle 5' water-improvement standard provide only a nominal legal-compliance check that legitimizes underlying inequitable land/water distribution without addressing historical dispossession, weak land-title enforcement, or industry lobbying to reclassify potable groundwater as non-potable to free it for irrigation use.
population: Sugarcane/ethanol industry stakeholders (farmers, union activists, local government officials, industry-association officials, refinery representatives, agronomists) and rural community residents in Valle del Cauca, Colombia
sample_size: 14 in-depth exploratory interviews (June-August 2012), plus additional interviews with an agricultural researcher and displaced small-scale-farming residents
effect_measure: Qualitative thematic analysis of 14+ in-depth interviews with industry and community stakeholders, applying Ribot & Peluso's theory of access; no statistical contrast
effect_estimate: The sugar industry holds 64% of surface-water concessions and 88% of underground-water concessions in the Valle del Cauca, compared to 26% and 2% respectively for household use, and pays lower rates than nearly all other user categories. Households in Candelaria and Pradera reported water shortages during dry/El Nino seasons attributed by an agricultural researcher to water being 'robbed by the sugar industry, and with license of CVC,' with water-use restrictions existing on paper but not enforced ('all the water management in Valle del Cauca is corrupt, CVC is co-opted by the sugar mills'). The sugar industry is actively lobbying to reclassify high-quality groundwater as non-potable specifically to remove it from household-use protections and free it for irrigation. Displaced small-scale farmers driven out by land concentration reported being forced to buy water for household use. Bonsucro's legalistic 'obey the law' certification standard is shown to legitimize this disproportionate access without addressing the underlying inequitable land/water distribution, weak land-title enforcement, or historical violent dispossession of peasant, indigenous, and Afro-Colombian communities.

citation: Boucher-Hedenström J, Rutherford D (2010). "Services d'eau et d'assainissement et dispersion « urbaine » dans le comté de Stockholm." Flux 2010/1-2 (n°79-80):54-68.
subnational_unit: Stockholm County, Norrtälje municipality case study
service_provider: Municipal water/sanitation utilities (commune-operated), individual/collective on-site alternative solutions, samfällighet (mini-network cooperative) associations
regulatory_model: Sweden's 2007 Water Services Act (Lag om allmänna vattentjänster) establishes municipal responsibility to provide water and sanitation service within a defined 'verksamhetsområde' (statutory service area) and mandates a cost-price (self-financing, no-profit) tariff principle for connected households. Outside the service area, households must arrange individual or collective alternative solutions, subject to municipal permit and inspection requirements; municipalities hold enforcement authority to require upgrade or closure of substandard individual installations. Four distinct service-configuration types (A-D) are identified, ranging from full municipal network connection to fully individual on-site solutions, with intermediate collective/cooperative (samfällighet) mini-network arrangements requiring unanimous consent among participating neighboring households to jointly connect to the municipal network or share a private system.
population: Households in Stockholm County's peri-urban and exurban sprawl zones, particularly in Norrtälje municipality, relying on a mix of municipal connection and individual/collective alternative water and sanitation solutions
sample_size: Qualitative interviews with named municipal/regional officials (Bertil Rusk, Håkan Jonsson) and the Bureau de planification régionale, combined with documentary/policy analysis
effect_measure: Qualitative institutional/policy case-study analysis (official interviews and documentary analysis); no statistical contrast
effect_estimate: An estimated ~90,000 households in Stockholm County rely on individual or collective alternative (non-municipal) water and sanitation solutions rather than a municipal network connection, reflecting the boundary of the statutory 'verksamhetsområde' service area under the 2007 Water Services Act. Four service-configuration types (A-D) are documented, with the mini-network (samfällighet) model requiring unanimous consent among neighboring households before a joint connection can be established -- a procedural/discretionary access barrier distinct from individual household eligibility. The cost-price tariff principle means connected households bear the full self-financing cost of network extension, creating an affordability dimension to the decision whether to seek municipal connection versus maintain an individual on-site solution.
model_type: qualitative policy/institutional case study (official interviews and documentary/regulatory analysis)
study_design: qualitative case study (interviews with named municipal and regional officials, combined with regulatory/documentary analysis) of municipal water/sanitation service configuration amid urban sprawl in Stockholm County, Sweden, with a Norrtälje case study
