citation: Baron C, Bonnassieux A (2013). "Gouvernance hybride, participation et accès à l'eau potable: Le cas des associations d'usagers de l'eau (AUE) au Burkina Faso." Annales de géographie 2013/5 (n°693):525-548.
subnational_unit: Rural and semi-urban communes covered by the Programme d'application de la Réforme (PAR), including the ADAE zone (southwest Burkina Faso) and Houndé
service_provider: Communes (municipalities), Water Users' Associations (AUE), private operators, ONEA (national water/sanitation utility, urban only), ADAE (associative operator)
regulatory_model: Burkina Faso's 2000 Reform of the rural/semi-urban water-infrastructure management system (Décret n°2000-514) and the 2001 Water Law (Loi n°002-2001/AN, recognizing a right to water without specifying volumes) together restructured governance following 2009 decentralization, which transferred water-infrastructure ownership and management competence (maîtrise d'ouvrage) from the State to communes. Water Users' Associations (AUE) require formal state homologation/licensing (agrément) as a condition of legal operation: territorial constitution at village/sector level, 30-80 members proportional to population, gender parity, a youth quota, and an elected 6-member bureau (president, secretary, treasurer, information secretary, 2 hygienists). AUE hold formal authority to set water tariffs for hand-pump (PMH) points, control point-of-service operators (fontainiers, gestionnaires de pompes), mediate local conflicts, and report to the commune on service disponibility/equity/quality. Simplified water-network (AEPS) management is delegated via affermage contracts to private operators or to associative structures (e.g. ADAE); communes may also delegate urban-adjacent service to ONEA.
population: Rural and semi-urban households and villages in Burkina Faso relying on Water Users' Associations, hand pumps (PMH), and simplified piped networks (AEPS) for drinking-water access; women and migrants as marginalized subgroups within AUE governance
sample_size: Qualitative field studies conducted under the ANR Sud II APPI research project (2011-2014), combining institutional/regulatory documentary analysis with village-level fieldwork
effect_measure: Qualitative institutional/policy case-study analysis (field studies, documentary and regulatory analysis); no statistical contrast
effect_estimate: AUE legal homologation criteria formally mandate gender parity and a youth quota among the 30-80 elected members, yet in practice women are systematically confined to subordinate 'hygienist' or treasurer roles within the 6-member bureau and rarely attain the presidency; migrants are frequently excluded from both water-management decision-making and, in some documented cases, from water access itself. Functionality data (PN-AEPA 2012) indicate only 63.6% of AUE are functional nationally, with functionality rates notably higher in the two regions managed by the associative ADAE model than in privately or state-delegated management zones. The 2000 Reform reduced AUE's formal role from full management of simplified networks (AEPS) to a narrower monitoring/oversight function once communes became infrastructure owners, though in practice some AUE (e.g. at Houndé) have retained broader de facto authority over both AEPS and hand-pump management.
model_type: qualitative policy/institutional case study (field studies, regulatory and documentary analysis, hybrid-governance conceptual framework)
study_design: qualitative case study (field studies conducted 2011-2014 under the ANR Sud II APPI project, combined with regulatory/institutional documentary analysis) of hybrid water governance and the legal-institutional role of Water Users' Associations in rural/semi-urban Burkina Faso

citation: Dwipayanti NMU, Nastiti A, Johnson H, Loehr J, Kowara M, de Rozari P, Vada S, Hadwen W, Nugraha MAT, Powell B (2022). "Inclusive WASH and sustainable tourism in Labuan Bajo, Indonesia: needs and opportunities." Journal of Water, Sanitation and Hygiene for Development 12(5):417-431.
subnational_unit: Labuan Bajo, Manggarai Barat Regency, East Nusa Tenggara Province
service_provider: PDAM (Perusahaan Daerah Air Minum, municipal water utility), local government (Planning Office, Health Office, Public Housing Office), hotel/tourism sector
regulatory_model: The municipal water utility PDAM supplies piped water sourced from springs on an intermittent (twice-weekly) schedule amid a documented supply deficit; Indonesia's Regulation of the Minister of Public Works No. 14/Prt/M/2010 sets a minimum water-requirement service standard of 60 L/person/day; PDAM applies a tiered tariff structure charging hotels a higher rate than households, ostensibly to promote conservation but with the documented unintended effect of preferential delivery to paying commercial users; the multi-stakeholder POKJA AMPL (Drinking Water and Environmental Health Working Group), coordinated by the Planning Office and including the Health Office, PDAM, and Public Housing Office, is the formal coordination forum for WASH governance but convenes irregularly; the National Total Sanitation Programme (STBM, implemented since 2012) governs sanitation-access improvement.
population: Local community households, hotel guests, hotel staff and management, and local/provincial government officials in Labuan Bajo, a 'super-premium' tourism destination
sample_size: 20 semi-structured interviews (10 female, 10 male; local government, hotel managers, community representatives, community health workers) and 6 focus groups with hotel staff (2-7 participants each), August 2020 fieldwork; 4-day validation workshop with 31 stakeholders, August 2021
effect_measure: Qualitative thematic content analysis (NVivo12, deductive plus inductive coding) of interview and focus-group transcripts; no statistical contrast
effect_estimate: Households in Labuan Bajo receive piped municipal water only twice per week amid a documented ~10 L/s supply deficit against total demand, with community water-service levels having decreased since 2015 despite substantial tourism-driven population and demand growth, while hotels maintain reliable supply via large onsite storage tanks households typically lack. A community midwife reported: 'if in the hotel [water utility] water flows every day, but in the community it almost never flows... we are paying for nothing, there is no running water.' The tiered tariff (hotels pay more per unit than households) was intended to incentivize commercial conservation but is perceived locally as producing preferential delivery to paying commercial users, generating documented risk of social conflict. Women bear disproportionate collection burden, waking at night/early morning for intermittent supply.

study_design: qualitative case study (20 interviews, 6 focus groups, 2020 fieldwork) of Inclusive WASH access, gender/disability equity, and water governance in the tourism destination of Labuan Bajo, Indonesia

subnational_unit: Cross River State: Calabar Municipality, Ikom, and Ogoja Local Government Areas

regulatory_model: Cross River State's new Water Supply and Sanitation Law (2025) establishes a statutory guarantee of access to basic WaSH services and creates a regulatory framework standardizing sector governance; the State Ministry of Water Resources inaugurated a dedicated WaSH regulatory department to monitor compliance and align service delivery with SDG 6; the 2025 WaSH Policy establishes sustainable-financing mechanisms, a public citizen-accountability WaSH dashboard, differentiated service delivery by locality, and sector professionalization; the State institutionalizes community task groups (e.g. Obubra LGA) as formal collective-governance mechanisms; the sector remains reliant on donor-supported programmes (e.g. USAID-funded borehole construction) alongside state funding shortfalls and institutional fragmentation.

effect_estimate: 79.0% of households rely on boreholes for water versus 21.0% on public taps/standpipes, reflecting limited formal piped-network coverage; 52.6% of households make 3-4 daily water-collection trips and 30.9% make 5+ trips; 79.0% report experiencing access challenges, primarily distance to source (48.1%) and water availability (31.6%); community participation in WaSH (72.7% overall) functions predominantly as unpaid monthly sanitation labor (82.8% of participatory activity) rather than financial contribution (2.6%), which the study interprets as community engagement substituting for, rather than complementing, limited state investment despite the 2025 statutory reform.

citation: Nkolola BN, Phiri A (2024). "From fetchers to decision-makers: exploring the gender dynamics of water access and governance in resource-poor communities of Mbala, Zambia." Journal of Water, Sanitation and Hygiene for Development 14(12):1291-1304.
service_provider: Water Point Committees (WPCs), NGO-drilled boreholes (UNICEF, SNV, USAID/SUNTA, World Vision International), Government funds (TRALAD, CDF)
regulatory_model: Water Point Committees (WPCs) are the community-level governance body responsible for managing water access points (WAPs, primarily NGO-drilled boreholes), with formal eligibility criteria for membership (age 18+, literacy, community trust, willingness to volunteer) and periodic elections; WPCs are responsible for organizing user-fee collection, contracting repairs, and holding community meetings, but lack any formal statutory backing, financial enforcement authority, or accountability mechanism beyond community consensus -- 53% of surveyed WPCs were non-functional at the time of study and 50.7% of households reported no requirement to contribute to WAP repairs, reflecting the absence of binding institutional enforcement of the community-management model.
population: Household heads, community leaders, and women/men engaged in water-related activities in rural Mbala district, Zambia
sample_size: 122 interviews (75.4% female, 24.6% male) via mWater tool version 3.0, purposive/criterion-based sampling, using the Empowerment in WASH Index (EWI)
effect_measure: Empowerment in WASH Index (EWI: empowerment ratio, disempowerment ratio, level of achievement) computed via R statistical software from 12-indicator survey, combined with qualitative thematic content analysis of interview transcripts
effect_estimate: Women scored substantially higher on the Empowerment in WASH Index than men (EWI 86.1% vs. 69.7%; empowerment ratio 67.4% vs. 30%), contradicting the study's initial hypothesis that women are marginalized from WPC decision-making. Instead, 53% of WPCs were reported non-functional and 50.7% of households reported no obligation to contribute financially to repairs, with the dominant reported reason for non-repair being 'there is no money' (over 50% of respondents) -- indicating that lack of enforceable financial-contribution mechanisms within the WPC governance structure, not gendered exclusion, is the primary driver of WAP non-sustainability. ~26% of WAPs were non-functional at time of data collection, with average breakdown frequency of every 2 weeks.
model_type: mixed-methods study (Empowerment in WASH Index survey quantification plus qualitative thematic content analysis)
study_design: mixed-methods study (122 mWater-tool interviews, EWI empowerment index, 2023-2024 fieldwork) of gender dynamics in Water Point Committee governance and WAP sustainability in rural Mbala, Zambia

citation: Mandara CG, Butijn C, Niehof A (2013). "Community management and sustainability of rural water facilities in Tanzania." Water Policy 15(S2):79-100.
subnational_unit: Kondoa and Mpwapwa districts, Dodoma region
service_provider: Village Water Committees (VWCs), private operators (PO) under VWC supervision, District Water Department (DWD)
regulatory_model: Tanzania's 2002 National Water Policy (NAWAPO) and 2008 National Water Sector Development Strategy (NWSDS) implement the 'subsidiarity principle' from Agenda 21, devolving full operation-and-maintenance cost-recovery responsibility to village-level Water User Committees (VWCs) financed through household user fees, while the District Water Department (DWD) retains formal technical-coordination and support responsibility but is documented to have only 41-50% of required technical staff and a pronounced deficit of plumbers, masons, and electricians in both study districts; VWCs are required to have gender-parity composition (equal male/female representation) under national guidelines; private-operator (PO) contracts are awarded via village-council-run tenders without District legal-unit involvement; the national frameworks are found not to explicitly define VWC or household-level roles and responsibilities, a documented statutory gap.
population: Households, Village Water Committee members, village council leaders, pump attendants, and District Water Department officials in nine villages across Kondoa and Mpwapwa districts, Tanzania
sample_size: 221-household survey (randomly selected), 6 focus group discussions (21 men, 18 women) in 2 villages, semi-structured interviews with village leaders and District Council officials, detailed case studies of 2 villages, October 2011-September 2012 fieldwork
effect_measure: Mixed-methods descriptive analysis (household survey frequencies, FGD thematic analysis, case-study comparison, and national-policy document review)
effect_estimate: The 221-household survey found a mean non-functionality duration of 4.3 months/year for village water infrastructure, with 20% of households reporting August-December as the peak non-functionality period and repair times ranging from half a day to three weeks. During breakdowns, households' most common coping responses were walking long distances (101 responses), experiencing multiple compounding problems (41), and having no water at all (35). In the detailed Chase-Chinyika case study, the village spent TSH 100,000-170,000 (~US$64-109) monthly on dry-season repairs, and villagers/leaders could not hold the DC-hired contractor accountable for an incomplete pump house/water tank despite repeated complaints to the DWD. In Seluka, the VWC's membership changed three times in 2011 alone due to disputes over lack of financial transparency, and the water fund account (reported at TSH 1,000,000/~US$640) had been inactive and unaudited since 2008, contributing to the collapse of six domestic distribution points and community reversion to unimproved hand-dug wells.
model_type: mixed-methods study (household survey, FGDs, semi-structured interviews, case studies, national-policy document review)
study_design: mixed-methods study (221-household survey, 6 FGDs, interviews, 2 detailed village case studies, 2011-2012 fieldwork) of community management, decentralization, and sustainability of rural water facilities in Kondoa and Mpwapwa districts, Tanzania

citation: Mbiza H, Scholz M, Dinka M, Hweru E (2026). "Service innovation and governance models for decentralised greywater systems in pro-poor urban settlements: evidence from Southlea Park, Zimbabwe." Water Policy 28(3):520-539.
urban_rural: peri-urban settlement under a Rural District Council (RDC)
service_provider: Households (decentralised greywater self-management), community-level cooperative systems, Rural District Council (RDC)/ward committee
regulatory_model: The Greywater Service Innovation Ladder (GSIL) is a proposed governance-oriented gate-based framework operationalising service-progression thresholds (GSMI, PRS, ESR, HPT indices) for household-to-community-to-utility-grade greywater service transitions; Zimbabwe's National Water Policy Review (2021) makes only limited reference to greywater management, creating a regulatory vacuum that leaves peri-urban settlements to manage wastewater informally; RDC/ward committees hold decision authority over Gate 1 (household-to-community) transitions while RDC-plus-regulator jointly hold authority over Gate 2 (community-to-micro-utility) transitions; the framework embeds affordability caps (Equity Safeguard Ratio, ESR) and rollback/pause mechanisms triggered if health or equity thresholds are not sustained.
population: Households in Southlea Park, a peri-urban settlement on Harare's southern periphery characterized by insecure tenure, no piped sewerage, and reliance on boreholes/shallow wells and on-site sanitation
sample_size: 150-household structured questionnaire survey (expenditure, equity, service reliability), plus environmental spot-measurements of greywater reuse/pooling practices and secondary policy/literature review
effect_measure: Composite governance-index scoring (GSMI 8-pillar composite 0-1, PRS 5-point ordinal, ESR ratio, HPT percentage) against predefined Gate 1/Gate 2 thresholds; descriptive baseline plus simulated incremental-improvement scenarios
effect_estimate: Baseline GSMI = 0.613, below the Gate 1 threshold of 0.70, driven by weaknesses in policy (0.55), finance (0.58), and data/monitoring (0.55) pillars; baseline PRS = 3 (meets Gate 1 minimum), ESR = 0.48 (1.9% of household income on greywater services, well within the 3-5% affordability threshold), HPT = 92% (meets Gate 1's 90% but not Gate 2's 95% threshold), reliability = 91% (near-pass for Gate 2's 93%). Simulation showed Gate 1 attainable within ~12 months via modest policy/equity/governance reforms (GSMI to 0.700), while Gate 2 required systemic multi-pillar restructuring (policy +0.20, finance +0.17, data/monitoring +0.18) to reach GSMI 0.750.
model_type: composite governance-index framework (GSIL) with baseline assessment and simulated incremental-improvement scenarios
study_design: mixed-methods case study (150-household survey, environmental spot measurements, policy document review) developing and applying a gate-based governance-maturity framework for decentralised greywater services

"Seeing sanitation: using photovoice for research and advocacy on WASH challenges in two Ethiopian urban primary schools." Journal of Water, Sanitation and Hygiene for Development 16(5):409-425.
subnational_unit: Jimma Town (Mendera Primary School and Seto Iddo Primary School)
service_provider: School administrations, local health authorities, local government (education, health, water, energy offices)

citation: Zhou S, Liang J (2021). Migrant workers and environmental amenities and infrastructure in urban China: from the lens of environmental justice. Journal of Environmental Policy & Planning 23(6):781-795.
service_provider: Municipal governments (wastewater and solid waste treatment infrastructure)
regulatory_model: China's household registration system (hukou), a legal/administrative status ascribed at birth determining permanent vs. temporary urban residency and eligibility for place-specific public services; central-government documents (National Development and Reform Commission, State Council) assigning municipal responsibility for pollution-treatment infrastructure provision; local governments' fiscal accountability limited to officially registered ('local-hukou-holder') populations
population: Urban populations of 290 Chinese prefecture-level cities, disaggregated by permanent vs. temporary (hukou-unregistered) residency status
sample_size: 290 cities, panel data 2008-2014 (1,577-1,769 city-year observations depending on model)
effect_measure: Panel fixed-effects regression (city and year fixed effects, clustered standard errors)
effect_estimate: A one-percentage-point increase in the share of temporary (hukou-unregistered) residents in a city is associated with a significant reduction of 0.00164 (10,000 m3/day)/10,000 persons in wastewater treatment capacity (p<0.01) and 0.0897 tons/day/10,000 persons in solid waste treatment capacity (p<0.01); also significant negative associations with the quantity of wastewater treated (p<0.1) and quantity of solid waste treated (p<0.1). For an average city of ~1.5 million people, this translates to a needed increase of 2,460 m3/day wastewater treatment capacity and 13.455 tons/day solid waste treatment capacity per 1-percentage-point increase in temporary residents merely to maintain the same per-capita service level. No significant association was found between temporary-resident share and public green space provision. A cross-sectional 2008-2014 change model and 1-2 year lag sensitivity tests corroborate the main findings.

covariates: Population density (logged), GRP per capita (logged), enrollment in high schools/colleges, unemployment rate, government spending per capita (logged)

subnational_unit: National, comparative case study of 3 countries' rural water sectors
service_provider: Community-based water management (CBWM) organizations: CAPS (Nicaragua), JAAs (Honduras), ASADAS/CAARS (Costa Rica); state agencies (INAA/DAR Nicaragua, SANAA/ERSAPS Honduras, ICAA Costa Rica)
regulatory_model: Nicaragua: 2010 Special CAPS Law (Law 722) formally recognizing rural water committees, following the incomplete 2007 National Water Law (Law 620); Honduras: 2003 General Framework Law for Water and Sanitation formally recognizing JAAs and creating regulator ERSAPS; Costa Rica: 1939 Law of Associations (Law 218) underlying ASADAS' legal status, plus the 1997-2000 CAARS-to-ASADA institutional transformation and a failed 2009 strengthening bill (Law 17324)
population: Rural community-based water management organizations and their member households across Nicaragua, Honduras, and Costa Rica
sample_size: Comparative documentary/policy analysis of 3 national CBWM sectors; cites national registration statistics (e.g. ~5,000 CAPS in Nicaragua; ~2,400 community water organizations in Costa Rica; JAA registration data for Honduras)
effect_measure: Comparative documentary/policy analysis; descriptive registration-rate statistics; no regression
effect_estimate: Nicaragua: within 5 years of the 2010 Special CAPS Law (Law 722), 30% of an estimated 5,000 national CAPS had formally registered; the 2007 National Water Law (Law 620) had explicitly overlooked CAPS' existence despite decentralizing water governance. Honduras: the 2003 Water Framework Law formally recognized JAAs, but 'a large proportion' had not registered with regulator ERSAPS nearly 20 years after passage, and of those registered only 'a minority' received full legal recognition; municipal governments were slow to receive their mandated 5% revenue share. Costa Rica: an estimated 1,820 of ~2,400 community water organizations (about 76%) held ASADA legal status under Law 218 as of the mid-2010s; in 2015 an estimated 40% of community water organizations were functioning outside the law. Across all 3 countries, formal legal recognition did not by itself resolve financial/technical capacity deficits or institutional fragmentation affecting rural water service sustainability.

sample_size: 282 community FGD participants (154 farmers + 128 women) + 33 of 47 Gram Panchayat heads + Block Development Officers/Agriculture Officers/Assistant Engineers from 6 Blocks
effect_measure: Descriptive frequency/percentage statistics from structured FGD and interview questionnaires across 3 governance levels; thematic/narrative qualitative analysis; no regression
effect_estimate: Over 90% of women respondents prioritized repair/maintenance of existing hand pumps; 82% prioritized installing more hand pumps; only 28% had access to piped water (2 of 16 villages). A documented caste-based exclusion mechanism: one woman reported 'We are not allowed to collect water from the handpumps located in the area where the upper castes people live. We have only one handpump for 64 households in our area.' Over 60% of women called for formal rules on equitable water allocation; one village (Neturia) had devised an informal queuing rule (first 5 households per 30-minute supply cycle) to ensure equitable access. Gram Panchayat heads and Block officials reported systematically higher funding availability for new-construction schemes than for repair/maintenance (a discretionary allocation pattern), and that installation-site hydrogeological surveys were 'completely overlooked,' contributing to frequent hand-pump non-functionality documented via photographic evidence (adjacent functional and non-functional hand pumps a few feet apart).
